articles.title: If Woke 1 Was Crazy, MAGA Woke Is Absolutely Insane
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: “Woke 1 was crazy.” Those four words, spoken on ABC’s This Week earlier this month by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, unexpectedly blasted open the doors of political discourse. For nearly two weeks, debate has raged in columns and on social media about the concept of “Woke 1” — whether there was indeed such a discrete era, how bad it really was, whether the broader left is allowed to simply laugh off the “woke” excesses of the era. Or to take the opposite tack, whether trying to move on from those excesses is an appalling betrayal of activist movements. Part of the problem is that for every five people talking about this, you’re likely to get six different explanations of what “Woke 1” actually means. Here’s mine: it’s the tut-tutting, puritanical style of progressive behavior, incubated in and spread from college campuses, that believed you could yell, condemn, finger-wag, and cancel your way to political change — and that reached its fever pitch in mid-to-late 2020, when we saw a spree of job losses and censorship on dubious grounds, because people were being yelled at, or because someone above them feared they eventually would be. This was a distinctly unproductive response to the mass outrage and protest over years of unaccountability for police murders, which demanded serious changes to American policing but ended up in part being diverted into censorship and policing of people’s behavior. The “Woke 1” excesses people are complaining about now, the people hurt by them, and the absurdities involved, were very real: A business school professor removed from teaching his own course and investigated for using a Mandarin word that sounds like a slur in English. A data analyst accused of “anti-blackness” and fired for posting research about the impact of different protest tactics on the Democratic vote. A biracial makeup artist fired for singing along to a rap song that has a well-known racial epithet in the lyrics. A Mexican American worker fired after a white motorist hallucinated him doing a white supremacist hand signal. This was on top of the wave of censorship that saw scenes , episodes , and entire shows and movies removed from streaming services for racial insensitivity, even when satirical. Online mobs condemned Paw Patrol for its positive depiction of police, and thousands of Twitter users angrily piled on the late Barbara Ehrenreich after they misconstrued one of her tweets as racist. Not to mention, there was an undeniable overall cultural vibe, effectively capitalized on by the Right, of censoriousness that the vast majority of people found repellant. But all of this is a very long windup to say that it’s a bit silly we’re still debating the woke excesses of 2020 and earlier, when we are right now , as you read this, going through a period of objectively much worse and more dangerous woke excess, with none of the same scrutiny. No, it’s not “Woke 2,” or some new version of left-leaning cancel culture that’s erupted again. This time, it’s the people who describe themselves as part of the pro-Trump, MAGA movement who are doing the canceling and taking far, far more radical steps to do it than we saw six years ago. Call it MAGA Woke. The Sequel Is Always Worse There are so many recent examples that it’s difficult to know where to begin. Remember when Trump and co. just searched a glossary of vaguely left-ish words — including “history,” “culture,” and “ climate ” — and then just mindlessly cancelled whichever grant or contract came up in the results, even if it screwed over their own voters? In the process of enforcing their own particular brand of political correctness, Donald Trump and the GOP defunded everything from research into diseases contracted by firefighters on September 11 and cancer studies , to Holocaust-related history projects and programs for disabled teens — all simply because they used words that made them uncomfortable. This was on top of scores of government workers placed on creepy public watch lists run by right-wing groups linked to the White House for the crime of having political opinions that offend the MAGA movement. At least half of those workers were forced on leave or ended up leaving their jobs. Nothing like any of this happened under what Trumpworld calls the “woke and weaponized” government run by Joe Biden. In fact, the big, bad, woke, cancel-culture scandal under that administration was that Twitter, both under government pressure but sometimes of its own accord, throttled the reach of some conservative accounts — a serious matter, but one that doesn’t nearly rise to the intensity and scale of the speech-related repression we’ve seen since Trump took office. Speaking of which, that tech censorship of Bad Opinions hasn’t stopped under Trump, even though he won promising to end censorship and signed an executive order supposedly doing just that. The only difference between the old regime and the new one is the targets: instead of anti-vaccine posts, social media censors now target abortion-pill providers, pro-Palestinian advocacy, anti-CEO comments, pro-LGBTQ posts, and more. In fact, MAGA has expanded its woke weaponization of social media beyond the digital realm, revoking people’s visas, denying them entry into the United States, pulling their travel privileges, and more because of posts and memes critical of Trump, his allies, or US policy. Worse by the Numbers This is all anecdotal, you might retort. But MAGA cancel culture isn’t worse because it feels like it is. We know it is, by the numbers. After the murder of right-wing influencer Charlie Kirk last year, Trump, his Vice President J. D. Vance, and their allies went on a cancel culture crusade, publicly demanding the heads of anyone daring to make utter a critical word about the late commentator — a speech stricture, by the way, that they themselves regularly violate. The result? More than six hundred Americans were fired, suspended, investigated, or otherwise disciplined by their bosses for saying things that triggered the White House and MAGA world, according to a review by Reuters, the majority of them educators, including fifty academics and top administrators at universities. Compare that to the twenty-two academics who lost their jobs in the “Woke 1” frenzy of 2020 and the 160 people fired for their pro-Palestinian advocacy over 2024 during the start of what we might call the “Watermelon Scare” — the ongoing and yearslong hysteria around, and resulting repression of, advocacy for Palestinian rights. Nor did those episodes see the threat of state power mobilized to try to get a comedian thrown off the air for personally offending a left-leaning politician, but this is exactly what happened after Kirk’s death, after Trump was angered by a joke late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel made. That intimidation effort against broadcast news networks is still ongoing , by the way. In other words, not only is “Woke 1” objectively not as bad as “MAGA woke,” it doesn’t even come close. In a separate Reuters analysis , the outlet found that the Trump administration was slapped down by federal judges — ten of them appointed by Republicans — in a whopping seventy-five First Amendment cases in his term so far, out of a total of ninety-three. By contrast, over the “woke and weaponized” Biden administration’s entire four years, federal judges weighed in on twenty-seven First Amendment challenges to its policies — a fraction of what Trump’s already racked up — and ruled against it in thirteen of those, or less than half, compared to Trump’s rate of 81 percent. Speaking of the Watermelon Scare, the crackdown on criticism of Israeli policy and defense of Palestinian justice is worse than ever under Trump. It turns out, somewhat bizarrely, that it’s criticism of the foreign country of Israel that is the most sensitive spot for the nominally America First movement. Donald Trump’s forces have arrested, locked up, and tried to deport, often successfully, hundreds of students merely for saying things that the MAGA movement finds offensive — specifically, criticism of Israel. It revoked one pro-Palestinian activist’s green card explicitly for criticizing Israel and is still trying to deport him today. Another activist had her visa revoked for cowriting an op-ed in her college newspaper criticizing the university’s response to the genocide in Gaza. They are just two of many. This has been condemned as dangerous and un-American across the board, by both the typically more left-leaning American Civil Liberties Union and the more right-leaning Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression . Both Trump’s administration and the MAGA movement behind him regularly conflate antisemitism with criticism of Israel — a conflation that is itself, by their own definition (“Holding Jews collectively responsible for actions of the state of Israel”), antisemitic. Using this dubious and offensive idea, Trump’s people have strong-armed universities into carrying out heavy-handed policing of what their students and faculty say, all in the name of protecting Jews on campus — by which they actually mean pro-Israel activists — from being offended. We know this is what they really mean, because it is Jews themselves who have often been targeted in this crusade, a form of pro-Israel cancel culture masquerading as a campaign against antisemitism. In fact, a whistleblower complaint just this week from within the Department of Justice laid out how much of this was driven not by actual concern about antisemitism but by MAGA world’s determination to cancel people for their pro-Palestinian speech. DOJ attorneys were, for instance, ordered to open an investigation into Columbia University based on a single New York Post article that detailed how protesters said and carried pro-Palestinian slogans and items. In another instance, investigators were ordered to do interviews with Middle East studies professors, Muslim ones in particular, at Brown University who had been accused of nothing, in order to trap them into saying something they could then call problematic. All of this has led to an unusual situation where — in the words of the Forward , a pro-Israel, Jewish publication — the Trump administration has both “sought to ban diversity measures meant to benefit minority groups, while in several cases requiring universities to create new policies to benefit Jews.” This is at the same time that cheerleaders for Trump’s cancel culture policies speak in language indistinguishable from “woke” progressive college students — like billionaire Bill Ackman, who complained about “how aggressive, intimidating, and disruptive [protests against the war in Gaza] could be to Jewish and Israeli students” and that “racism against white people has become considered acceptable by many.” This form of MAGA wokeness hasn’t just negatively impacted the Left. It has also boomeranged on Trump’s own movement, as when figures serving or appointed to serve in his administration were thrown out for their criticism of Israel, which a rival political faction within Trump’s movement cynically mislabeled as antisemitism. Ironically, several out-and-out antisemites continue to serve in prominent positions under Trump with none of the same objection from this faction — because just like with “Woke 1,” the exponents of MAGA Woke often use cynical accusations of bigotry as a way to litigate completely separate political disagreements. Let’s Have Some Perspective The excesses of “Woke 1” were very real and unhelpful, which the Left has to acknowledge if it wants to be able to move on from that period. But it doesn’t hold a candle to the frenzy of MAGA-driven wokeness that we are in the middle of right now, where it’s not just the private sector bringing the hammer down on workers who offend Trump and his movement but where the far-reaching use of state power is punishing and even criminalizing people for speech that MAGA figures regard as politically incorrect. Those efforts have seen people locked up, fired, doxed, exiled from the country, and even criminally prosecuted for their speech. This is all objectively worse than anything that happened in 2020–21. It would be good if, in between obsessing over dumb, years-old tweets about Thanksgiving and whiteness, the media grilled Trump-backed candidates about some of it.

articles.title: Canada’s Socialists Are Coming for City Hall
articles.author: James Adair
articles.content: In October, a majority of Canadians will face the choice of electing new city councils across Canada. Of this majority, only a fraction will actually make the trek to the schools, churches, and legions that host polling stations. Characterized by perpetually low turnout — often hovering around 30 percent — Canadian municipal elections attract far less engagement than their provincial and federal counterparts. One possible explanation for this disengagement is the limited power of Canadian municipal governments. Canadian municipalities exist in an oddly subordinate position. As “ creatures of the provinces ,” they possess only those powers provincial governments grant them. As a result, municipal decisions are often downstream of what provinces allow — and can be overturned almost at will. Conservative provincial governments have in fact made it routine practice to attack the autonomy and decision-making capacity of cities. Doug Ford, current Conservative premier of Ontario and brother of the infamous former mayor of Toronto, has, in his time, forcefully cut the size of Toronto’s city council and decided that specific municipal bike lanes (on his route to work) were illegal and ordered them torn up. City councils have historically been parochial institutions: the domain of landlords, businessmen, and the occasional bleeding-heart liberal. But this time around, there is a groundswell of socialists running across Canada. And some are serious contenders. Universal Snow Clearing “Universal snow clearing” seems almost like a parody of what a Canadian socialist running for municipal office would campaign on. But for Damian Mikhail , who is running for Waterloo Ward Six, it made sense. Harsh winters and inconsistent — or a complete lack of — snow clearing means that walking around becomes basically impossible. “That universal snow clearing argument has tended to be quite universally liked. Among young families and seniors, especially,” Mikhail told Jacobin . Mikhail was formerly the president of the Waterloo University Student Association as well as cochair of the Ontario New Democratic Party youth wing. His first major foray into politics was fighting to “return night transit to Waterloo and stop cuts to the local LRT [light rail transit]” through the New Democratic Party campus club. Ward Six contains the University of Waterloo but also extends into established residential neighborhoods, creating sharp divisions between the student areas and nonstudent areas, as well as between renters and homeowners. The challenge for Mikhail will be running up the vote count in the student neighborhoods while remaining competitive elsewhere. Turning out students — notoriously difficult to mobilize in municipal elections — will be a challenge in and of itself. Damian Mikahil was formerly the president of the Waterloo University Student Association as well as cochair of the Ontario New Democratic Party youth wing. (Courtesy of Damian Mikhail for Ward 6) Mikhail is prioritizing door-knocking over digital communication. He says he has already knocked on every door in the ward and encountered a positive response. The last election’s turnout was 23 percent, and the incumbent won with only 896 votes cast. Mikhail’s platform — three policies that can fit on the back of a postcard — reflects a trend toward a kind of socialist minimalism. In addition to universal snow clearing, he proposes a renters’ protection office “with a mandate for proactive and consistent inspections of rentals in the city and to report on the issues plaguing renters,” as well as a municipal housing corporation that will function as both a public builder and housing operator. The policy, if enacted, could begin to reshape housing in Waterloo. Despite its avowedly socialist character, Mikhail presents it as less an ideological project than a demonstration of the possible strengths of a municipal government willing to flex its muscles. “This is actually a conversation we have had as a campaign team. How ideological do we want our kind of framing to be? I’m Palestinian, and a lot of my organizing has been around Palestinian [liberation]. . . . I’m obviously a very kind of partisan person in many senses.” Mikhail said. “But the conversation that we wanted to have is that there . . . tends to be a belief that nothing is possible, that change isn’t possible, that the government can’t really do anything for you. “What we want to do with our platform is give very concrete actions that the city can take that will just improve your life, and the idea for that is, from a more philosophical perspective, is to show the people of Waterloo that you can expect something from your government, that your government should be actively improving your life.” Waging the Class War Solomon Yi-Kieran , another student organizer turned candidate, has been campaigning since February — first for the nomination to run on the Coalition of Progressive Electors (COPE) party line, and now as one of the party’s five candidates running for city council. “One of the benefits of a long campaign is that it has been amazing to see just how much momentum we’ve been building when we’re out there. . . . I went from being a student organizer whose base was mainly other students to being able to go to any part of the city, do a canvass, and get recognized by every couple of people when I’m out there.” Solomon Yi-Kieran has blended together a folksy charm and a militant attitude to produce a constant deluge of videos. (Courtesy of Solomon Yi-Kieran for City Council) Vancouver is unique among major Canadian cities in having a well-established municipal party system. This provides some advantages: the formalized party form allows socialist candidates to organize throughout the year and forge strong connections with social movements that, in turn, help promote all their candidates. But COPE, Vancouver’s oldest active left-wing party, has won the mayor’s seat and a council majority only once, in 2002. For much of the 2010s, it had no representation on council and was generally considered to be in decline. Then in a 2025 by-election, the city elected Sean Orr — a democratic socialist, dishwasher, and punk vocalist. His victory helped COPE mount a resurgence. Yi-Kieran is emblematic of COPE’s renaissance. Young, social media savvy, and avowedly a radical. Yi-Kieran has blended together a folksy charm and a militant attitude to produce a constant deluge of videos. In contrast to Mikhail’s minimalism, Yi-Kieran embraces a more wide-ranging politics, campaigning on everything from more municipal Wi-Fi hotspots and universal metro cards to banning surveillance pricing. It fits the Vancouver ecosystem of young, downwardly mobile students and graduates who are tapped in online. “If we as socialists want to be educating voters, given the kind of horrifically low turnout for municipal elections, we need to be using social media to connect with people in an organic and genuine way.” Yi-Kieran believes. “No matter what policy we’re talking about, the same through lines are always there. It is about equitable access to good services, no matter what part of the city you live in. . . . It is about making sure that we have a government that is listening to people.” One of Yi-Kieran’s principal challenges will be the uniqueness of Vancouver’s electoral system. A candidate’s prospects are tied partly to the fortunes of the party, but councilors are also elected at-large rather than ward-by-ward. Rather than representing specific areas or constituencies, each elector votes for up to ten candidates from across the city. It makes campaigning much harder. “As someone who takes transit and does not drive, you need to go to literally every part of this city for campaigning. It is definitely a challenge.” “I spend a lot of time on public transit,” Yi-Kieran joked, “but at the same time, I’ve also really enjoyed the way I’ve gotten to campaign within this system. In that, I am literally going to every corner of the city. I am becoming intimately familiar with every single neighborhood.” Yi-Kieran, who says their dream job would be a high school teacher, has embraced a rhetoric of class war. In their acceptance speech for the COPE nomination, Yi-Kieran embodied the renewed vigor of COPE. “We didn’t start this class war, but we’re going to win it.” Chiara Padovani Few candidates in Canada have taken the fight to landlords as directly as Chiara Padovani . A tenant organizer and social worker who helped lead one of Toronto’s largest-ever tenant strikes , Padovani is running for city council in York South–Weston (YSW). Unlike Mikhail and Yi-Kieran, Padovani has run before. She ran in 2022, coming within ninety-four votes of unseating incumbent Frances Nunziata, whose office was later found guilty of using city resources to campaign, a violation of the city’s code for councilors. Padovani’s campaign didn’t end with her defeat. During the race, Padovani had turned her office into a local organizing hub, distributing tenant’s guides door-to-door and helping establish a building-based tenant union. Afterward she was concerned that losing the physical space would slow the nascent organizing effort in YSW. YSW, a deeply racialized, quickly gentrifying, and high-density tenant area, was a prime spot for such organizing. “I called up about 200 of my election supporters who had contributed to my campaign to run for city council, and I told them I really want to try to keep the office open,” Padovani said. She asked if people could chip in CA$5 or $10 a month. It worked. She was soon able to guarantee enough reliable income from monthly donations to extend the lease. It has been “the foundation of resourcing this movement, just by having a physical space in the community where people can meet and organize.” What began as a campaign has since become more durable. It is now an organization operating between electoral and movement work and building a measure of worker power in YSW. “You can’t run an election on a socialist mandate for tenants’ rights if you’re not organizing the tenant community and getting concrete material wins for them to have some faith that things can change.” There is a confidence and professionalism to Padovani’s current campaign, refined through years of organizing. In many respects, Padovani has acted as YSW’s shadow councilor — hosting community skate events, dealing with constituency work, and building a strong foundation for her current run. Consequently, the campaign feels almost like an incumbent run. But that just reflects the strength of the movement Padovani has helped build in a corner of Toronto. The first campaign fed into the movement, and now the movement feeds back into the campaign. “Between the electoral campaign and the organizing campaigns, we’re not doing this to make a point. We’re doing it to win. We need to win material differences in people’s lives. Like, this is what’s at stake. If I wanted to just make points, I would be on Twitter all day, right?” The Inheritance of 1919 The Winnipeg General Strike of 1919 transformed Canada’s socialist and labor movements. But it wasn’t until 1934 that Winnipeg elected its first socialist mayor and, with him, a labor-controlled city council. It was a rare victory for Canadian municipal socialists. Sewer socialism never found its footing here as it did south of the border. Instead, political energy was focused on winning provincial governments and chasing the dream of a socialist prime minister. There are many reasons for the renewed interest in municipal socialism: The worsening housing crisis , the cost-of-living crisis , and the growing failure of government to address either. But Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York City has altered what people perceive as the political horizon. Winning power locally has never seemed more possible. Winnipeg’s 1934 socialist city council would be the last. It was a disappointing experience for many. Unable to make significant changes, the movement fell apart. Winning is not a guarantee of victory. But a victory from either Mikhail, Yi-Kieran, or Padovani would establish a beachhead for a different kind of Canadian city — one capable of proving that government can materially improve people’s lives.

articles.title: Liberalism’s Cult of the Individual Has Failed Us
articles.author: Dustin Guastella
articles.content: Is it better to “ bowl alone ” than to join anything that smacks of a sect? Were the New Deal’s Works Progress Administration and Civilian Conservation Corps, which put millions to work rebuilding their country, just state-sanctioned “cults?” According to one prominent liberal: maybe! In an article entitled “No, Senator Murphy, I don’t want to join your cult,” Jerusalem Demsas, the liberal publisher of The Argument magazine, goes after Democratic Senator Chris Murphy for daring to argue that we ought to have some shared social commitment to the public good. For Murphy, Americans — particularly young men — are living through an epidemic of loneliness that’s not only corroding our democracy but destroying the social bonds that hold our society together. These men, particularly those without college degrees, are increasingly isolated and adrift post-COVID: they’ve fallen out of the labor force, they’re not having kids, they’re absent in their communities, and basically going nowhere fast. Social scientists are starting to take note. Last spring, researchers at the University of Virginia’s Karsh Institute of Democracy published a report entitled Nobody to Call , the product of dozens of interviews with young men without college degrees. The report is devastating. When asked if they participate in any kind of social or community activities, their responses are bleak: “No, I do not. Except for my family, I don’t regularly do anything with anybody,” as one interviewee puts it. Another: “No, I can’t say I do. I would like to get into some extracurricular activities, but work [takes] a lot of my time.” And another: “No, not really. I used to go fishing, but that’s it. . . . I used to go to church a lot. I don’t do that no more, and I ain’t never been part of a club or anything like that.” Zoomers, the Low-Trust Generation The result of all this disaffiliation is an exceptionally low-trust generation. The General Social Survey recently asked Americans if most people could, in fact, even be trusted. Their answers depended entirely on when they were born: the Silent Generation (born just before World War II) had the highest levels of trust, with 41 percent agreeing that “most people can be trusted” and 51 percent instead saying “you can’t be too careful in dealing with people.” For Gen Z, only 13 percent agreed that most people could be trusted and a whopping 74 percent answering “you can’t be too careful.” This raises a big question: How do progressives plan on winning the kinds of transformative social policies they campaign on, policies that presuppose a strong degree of social trust, if the next generation of Americans have so very little of it? None of this is a surprise to Murphy. The senator from Connecticut recently published a book on the subject, The Crisis of the Common Good: The Fight for Meaning and Connection in a Broken America . You don’t have to have read it to agree that when it comes to the “common good” we do, indeed, have a crisis on our hands. Demsas agrees too — she even praises Murphy for making a sustained political argument instead of using the book as campaign propaganda. Yet Demsas thinks Murphy is nuts to call for a “cult of the common good” — which she likens to an actual cult. Whatever Murphy is arguing, it’s clear he doesn’t want to sign everyone up for Heaven’s Gate. The “cult” language is certainly a provocation, meant to juxtapose our neglect of the common good with the popular cults of profit and technology regularly celebrated in the business press. No doubt Demsas knows as much, but she nonetheless tries to paint Murphy as part of some lunatic fringe. Why? Murphy, it should be said, is among the very few senators who have actually acknowledged the widespread feeling of anomie and alienation growing in our society. Recently, he garnered headlines for calling attention to the ways in which private equity had taken over youth sports, even preventing parents from filming their kids’ hockey games. Since at least the mid-century, according to political scientists like Robert D. Putnam, Americans have been sliding down a slope of ever-increasing loneliness. In just the past half century, community bonds have dissolved, romantic love has become harder to come by, church pews have emptied out, associations have atrophied, labor unions have been crushed, and whole towns have been hollowed out by deindustrialization. During that same period, the rich have gotten richer, markets have grown wider, and technological progress has taken off. To fill this void, we’ve been fed a steady diet of social media and cheap consumer goods. It doesn’t seem to be working out so well. The result is that, according to new research reviewed by the Financial Times , “on an average day in 2023, one in 10 young Americans aged between 23 and 29 did not spend a single minute interacting face to face with another person.” But according to Demsas, we’re not meant to talk about that. Just go to church, she argues. Literal Witch Hunts? To be sure, Murphy is no socialist, let alone a radical. Yet he at least understands that Democrats — or better yet, Americans — need more than just “abundance” if they are to have any chance of fixing this country’s profound social problems. Demsas’s polemic, on the other hand, reveals a kind of harrowing fear about Murphy’s concerns. She likens his call for a renewed public commitment to the common good to a literal witch hunt. Here’s Demsas: Now, obviously, I don’t think Murphy supports hanging women for witchcraft. Nor does punishing someone for price gouging necessarily lead to witch trials. But it’s also not an accident that a community with enough coercive power to punish someone for charging a lot for nails ends up using that coercive power in other realms of life as well. The regulation of prices, religious orthodoxy, and women’s behavior all stemmed from the same view: that “the community” could define the good, interpret dissent as moral disorder, and punish the dissenter. The crux of her argument here is that no demos could ever satisfactorily define the common good. Live and let live — and let everyone’s individual consumer preferences be catered to, regardless of the damage done. But here’s the thing: we are already living Demsas’s dream. The America of the 2020s is largely her world, not Murphy’s. And it’s her version of liberalism that is hegemonic, not Murphy’s. Where today do we find widespread, stultifying traditionalism? Excluding ultrareligious sects, where can you even find these overbearing “communities” she fears? In fact, most Americans complain about the opposite problem. The rise of antisocial behavior and the inability of the “community” (or whatever is left of it) to enforce even basic social norms. Today our political subjectivity is thoroughly neoliberal: atomized, asocial, and acquisitive. According to research sponsored by the Wall Street Journal and NORC, the only social value that has increased in popular appeal since 2020 is how much we see “money” as of paramount importance. America no longer has citizens, just consumers. Markets and Consumer Choice Can’t Fix the Crisis of Loneliness and Meaninglessness Still, the trouble is, according to Demsas, that while liberalism “begins with the presumption of freedom,” Murphy “begins with an Official Version of the Good Life.” This is untrue. Of course liberalism has its own version of the Good Life: it is found in Demsas’s unflinching defense of individual autonomy, echoing Isaiah Berlin’s concept of “negative liberty.” For liberalism, the highest good is the freedom of the individual to express their desires however they choose, so long as that desire doesn’t inhibit another. Importantly, as Demsas is careful to note, this entails a wide degree of economic liberalism — the freedom of markets. Yet what happens when this kind of freedom has liberated us from the very bonds that hold us together as a society? What happens when markets have dissolved so much of what we share in common that we’re left as strangers? Are liberals prepared to argue that contemporary market society is good simply because we are free to buy cheap junk on Amazon? I suspect much of what lies behind Demsas’s surprisingly vituperative reaction to the mild-mannered senator is that Murphy has been vocal about America’s broken economic system. He is a major critic of globalization , whereas Demsas sees no problem in importing cheap Chinese cars , American jobs be damned. Murphy thinks the financial sector is bloated, shamelessly corrupt, and a drag on broad prosperity. Demsas claims it’s “dead wrong” to blame the housing crisis on Wall Street. Murphy argues against Big Tech’s overweening influence. Demsas says, if you don’t like tech’s influence over our politics and our social lives, or its corrosive effect on our collective psyche, just buy different junk . Ultimately, Murphy is a critic of atomizing individualism and “the loss of connection to, and identification with, community,” a tendency encouraged by the unfettered marketization of everything. For Demsas, well, community doesn’t matter much . As she puts it, “this idea that repeat interactions with a lot of people that you are in community with is the foundation of a good democracy, a good society, a place where people will donate their kidneys to one another, because they know each other . . . I just don’t think that’s true.” A lot of Demsas’s objections are also downstream from the larger divide in the Democratic Party. Demsas is a partisan of the Abundance faction, while Murphy is more of a populist. As Vincent Bevins insightfully notes , any visitor to this country can see that America has already chosen abundance. Remember all the European World Cup tourists freaking out about the size of our gas stations? The infinite supply of cheap, hot food? No one would deny that America excels at growing its economy — the trouble is that since at least the 1970s, we’ve been terrible at sharing the abundant harvest in anything like a fair distribution. The professional class has pulled further and further away from the working class in terms of income and assets, meanwhile the superrich are in another world entirely. The resulting asset-based K-shaped economy is no doubt responsible for much of the widespread social dysfunction. Affluent liberals could almost be forgiven for not seeing how dire the situation has become. In professional social circles, all seems well for the most part; they’re still somewhat insulated from the worst of it. Affluent professionals still enjoy long stable marriages. They still have large friend groups. They’re more likely to go to church. And now, according to a new paper by Jesús Fernández Villaverde and Patrick Norrick, the rich may even be having more kids than the working class and the poor — a trend that would have been unthinkable just a few decades ago. When parenthood and even friendship become luxury goods, something has gone seriously wrong. Maybe then we need social policies that bring people together to help reform those bonds? And yet all of Demsas’s fearmongering about the danger of Big Government coercion — no doubt the liberal version of the Right’s “I will not eat the bugs ! I will not live in the pod!” — is leveraged against Murphy’s policy proposal: a program to send young people around the country on public service missions for half a year. This is his supposedly intolerable “cult-like” agenda. What exactly is wrong with this? If anything, the plan is far too modest. Yet for Demsas, it’s a gross overreach. Small-bore “nudges” are fine, she says, but the state should basically stay out of the business of trying to influence any prosocial behavior. Presumably only the market is qualified to shape our social behaviors. Demsas concludes that “Politics shouldn’t create meaning, it should make room for it.” That sounds good, as far as it goes. The trouble is that politics — that is, the kind of politics Demsas favors (more markets, more choices) — has produced a degraded public sphere and an epidemic of anomie. The power of the market in America, unique among developed nations for its lack of buffering social democratic institutions, has crowded out everything else. Our economy , structured as it is, has radically reduced our opportunities for genuine social communion, and in that way it has radically reduced our opportunities for developing shared commitments. It’s made us selfish and shortsighted. Maybe that’s no problem for liberalism, but it is for democracy. Democracy depends on our shared commitments to one another as much as it does on our ability to express dissenting beliefs. After all, a commitment to some minimum level of shared social morality — one might even call it an “Official Version of the Good Life” — certainly inspired framers like James Madison, who argued: “To suppose that any form of government will secure liberty or happiness without any virtue in the people, is a chimerical idea.” And it turns out there is virtue in the people. Most Americans agree that we ought to live in a society where people can retire with dignity, where they can form and sustain a marriage, raise a couple kids in a home they own, all in a safe neighborhood. This is what most Americans understood as a normal life for generations. Today it’s a luxury product. Getting back to that norm starts with rebuilding social trust. At least Murphy is trying to figure out ways to do so. In the end, it’s liberalism, enthralled to a cult of the individual, that cannot see the reality of widespread social alienation in this country. And Demsas’s preferred politics will do little more than help “make room” for more opportunities to check out.

articles.title: It’s Prime Time for Socialists. How We Make Our Case Matters.
articles.author: Ben Burgis
articles.content: If a store where you live still carries newspapers, you can try a little experiment. Pick up the most recent issue of the New York Times or the Wall Street Journal or the New York Post or the Washington Post . Start flipping through the pages, and see how many seconds it takes you to find the word “socialist” in a headline. In August 2026, this won’t be a very time-consuming experiment. Since Zohran Mamdani became mayor of the most important city in the capitalist world, socialism has been a hot topic. Now several other Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members have won their primaries and are likely headed to Congress, putting socialists even more in the spotlight. DSA conferences are getting long write-ups in mainstream national publications. Cable news hosts are eagerly seeking out socialists to defend their ideas. When DSA put out a new platform document, the Speaker of the House denounced it on the floor of Congress. This explosion of visibility has come with some growing pains. Democratic socialism was long a marginal force in American politics, if it was even in the mix at all. Where in the last several decades we’ve become far too accustomed to mostly talking about our ideas to each other, we are now speaking before a general audience. Much of our political program is relatively straightforward. Some socialist policies, like Medicare for All and reducing the workweek to thirty-two hours, are already quite popular . When we say that the fight against the Trump administration’s disturbing authoritarianism needs to be linked to a broader project to curb the political and economic power of the wealthy, and that the Democratic Party establishment is very much part of the problem, many ordinary Americans are prepared to listen. In other ways, though, we have a steeper hill to climb. Even the chunk of the public that most aligns with our short-term goals has not yet been won over to our long-term vision. We’re socialists because we don’t just want a better social contract for the working class within capitalism in the short term, although we certainly do want that. We understand that whatever reforms we win now can be rolled back tomorrow if wealthy business owners are allowed to hold onto their structural power in our economy, and thus continue to influence our politics. To both secure the gains already won and remedy the core injustice that structures our society, socialists contend that society’s productive assets must eventually come under collective and democratic ownership. This vision lies entirely outside the map of “normal” political disagreement in our society. We’re raising fundamental issues with exploitation and ownership that traditionally haven’t been considered up for debate. That means that our ideological opponents’ go-to move is always going to be to portray us as insane, out-of-touch ultraradicals. And if we lack rigorous thought and discipline around the less persuasive and defensible ideas floating around the socialist movement, we only make our opponents’ job easier. Breaking Bad Habits During the long decades when socialists were unaccustomed to having to justify ourselves to anyone but one another, we had many incentives to take whatever positions felt the most hard-line. When political power seems permanently out of reach, politics becomes reduced to a kind of symbolic moral protest. And if that’s all it is, there’s nothing left but to lodge the purest protest we can manage. Instead of trying to persuade those who are, if not actually right-wing, at least to our right (that is, the vast majority of the public), we got in the habit of spending our time trying to prove our leftist bona fides to those who might outflank us to the left. We picked up many bad habits during this long sojourn in the political wilderness — habits that we still need to do much more to shed. Most of the new DSA platform, for example, is excellent , but it includes multiple lapses into dubious maximalism, on subjects ranging from borders to policing and prisons . DSA-affiliated politicians who have to worry about defending their positions to voters have declined to defend those elements of the platform. This in turn has led some socialists to argue about how to hold such politicians “accountable.” But it might be more politically productive to take a beat to consider the possibility that our political instincts need correcting. It’s a reasonable aspiration for a socialist organization to want to build firm consensus around a series of core ideas, such that we would then withdraw support from officeholders who deviate too much from that consensus. But it’s not realistic to first throw all sorts of radical-sounding but half-baked ideas onto the pile and then try to build a firm consensus around the whole thing. No one denies that there are genuine points of principle that need to be defended even when they’re unpopular. Even there, we must think carefully about which fights to pick, and how to express unpopular but genuinely vital principles in a way that makes them as appealing as possible to the people we’re trying to win over. But the worst-case scenario is one where socialists feel we need to prove our radical credentials to each other by defending positions that are not only unpopular but genuinely poorly thought-out. What, for example, does it mean to say, as DSA’s national platform does, that various laudable and desperately needed criminal justice reforms should be understood as steps toward “abolishing” police and prisons? Even in an advanced socialist society where poverty was something people read about in history books, at least some interpersonal violence would almost certainly still persist. When it does, investigation by some sort of professionalized, publicly administered law enforcement body followed by trials and involuntary confinement for those found guilty is a far better solution than vigilantism, vendettas, or ultralocalized community groups deciding who’s guilty and what they think counts as a fair punishment à la medieval villages. If what we really mean by “abolition” is that we want the corrupt and brutal forms of policing and prisons that exist now to be replaced by more humane and democratic versions of law enforcement in a socialist future, expressing this as a call for “abolition” is misleading on the substance of the proposal, since we aren’t actually calling to abolish policing and prisons but rather to change them. It is also flagrant political malpractice, as any average person who hears “abolish police and prisons” imagines a world overrun by theft and violence with no recourse. And rightly so, as the term “abolish” means to eliminate immediately and entirely, which was the position of nineteenth-century abolitionists toward the institution of slavery. When some DSA spokespeople go on large media platforms and bite the bullet on every wildly unpopular and poorly thought-through maximalist idea that’s arisen in our movement — cheerfully affirming that, yes, we do want that — it’s an easy way to win points for loyalty and radical commitment within the circles of the already converted. But it’s a very bad strategy for making our case to a broader public. Recently, Jacobin contributor and DSA member Eric Blanc made these very points in a WNYC interview with host Brian Lehrer. “It’s frankly just a mistake that national DSA took certain positions that are both marginalizing for us in the short term and just politically wrong even in the long term,” Blanc said. “In what world does it make sense, if our goal is to organize millions of people and to overcome the Democratic establishment and to defeat Trumpism, to take a position that you know is just going to give fuel to your opponents, and for which there’s no practical upshot right now? Taking that sort of doctrinaire ideological position seems to me a reflection of a lack of experience and a lack of engagement in mass politics.” He’s exactly right. It’s Showtime There are many existing institutions that we really could and should “abolish” in the short or medium term. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, for example, is a brutal agency that Donald Trump has increasingly wielded as a kind of private army. It’s also a relatively recent addition to the American state. Anyone who can remember what life was like in the 1990s should be able to imagine its abolition. The US Senate, of course, is vastly better entrenched, but it’s also deeply undemocratic, and DSA and other socialists have rightly called for getting rid of it. Those are the kinds of arguments any socialist interested in publicly defending our movement should be prepared to take up on Fox News or anywhere else. But we unnecessarily make the task of persuasion harder when we let our enemies present these positions as part of a package deal with far murkier and less defensible demands. Similarly, if we’re trying to argue that the failures of authoritarian state socialism in the twentieth century shouldn’t mean that capitalism is the best humanity will ever be able to do, and that a better form of socialism is possible and desirable, we don’t do ourselves any favors by refusing to say anything too negative about left-wing dictatorships targeted by US foreign policy. Oftentimes, this reluctance is motivated not by sympathy for the political systems of the targeted countries but by fear of “conceding” something to neocons and warmongers. The problem is that this does exactly nothing to reassure anyone that we really are committed on principle to free speech and multiparty democracy. It also makes the warmongers’ task easier by giving them fodder to portray everyone who opposes imperial aggression against these countries as a stealth supporter of their systems. The points we should be relentlessly making instead are that societies are far less likely to liberalize when they’re faced with external threats, and in any case US policy should focus on what the United States can reasonably bring about — alleviating suffering by dropping sanctions and normalizing relations. This is the line DSA cochair Ashik Siddique took during a recent grilling on CNN about Cuba: “Many decades of US policy at this point have shown that if we want to expand democracy across the world, military regime change and economic blockades are not the way to do it.” The consistent thread running through all these particular examples is a simple one. We have a chance to rally broad support behind our short-term social democratic agenda, and to slowly and steadily build support for a more radical socialist horizon. But we can only do that if we think seriously at every stage about exactly what we want, how to get it, and how to assemble a popular majority behind it. This is a completely different mindset than one where we spend our time trying to reassure one another of our radical commitment. We need to act like America is watching, because it is.

articles.title: Abolishing Gender Essentialism
articles.author: Cleveland DSA
articles.content: Gender is a historical process. It is not the same thing from century to century, decade to decade, or even moment to moment. At one point, archers used high heels to get an advantage on the battlefield, leggings were worn by royalty, pink used to be seen as a ‘guys’ color because it was calm and collected, they used to think it was manly to put rainbows on trucks, and makeup used to be for everyone, before in the 20 th century the fashion industry made these things marketed to women. Historical performances of gender are not the same throughout time and culture – in other words they are not essential to a person, they are something which can be undermined, and change throughout a person’s life. No person is essentially any gender, because gender is a performance. That does not mean that people do not express themselves as one gender or another, or cannot continue to do so, it means that gender is so variable that it cannot be boiled down to a binary. The reason that it’s so valuable for reactionaries to focus on issues such as binary gender, and create such an essentialist paradigm for gender, is because the ruling class want to use it as an scapegoat to advance the agenda of brainwashing people with transphobia, so that they can uphold an American exceptionalist facade. The goal is to cover over all the genocide, the patriarchy, and the white supremacy, which is the United Snakes of Amerika. Every person is a multiplicity of gender expressions, and this is “micro transsexuality” that Deleuze and Guattari talk about in “Anti-Oedipus.” Gender expression and gender identity are also separated, and have no necessary relation to each other. That means that if you identify as a man, you could behave in mostly what your era deems feminine, and this has no relation to what a person could identify as. The identity and the expression are chosen, not innate, and they can be arbitrarily undermined by any variable expression, which occurs in thousands, if not millions, or more, at every second. Gender as a historical process What we think of as gender changes from moment to moment. As a historical process, gender is part of change, and flux, as opposed to a constant fixed thing in the past like Heidegger’s notion of being. Gender might be thought of as coterminous, happening with and at the same time as time itself. Gender and time can be thought of contrasted to queerness as a rupture with the continuum of time. Gender, through history, has been a process of capture into a submissive role in Europe, through the middle ages when women were vilified and seen as witches. Witches were actually women that had set up their own crafts and shops according to Butch Lee in “Military Strategy for Women and Children.’ Women, likewise, according to Abdullah Ocalan were subjugated by religious leaders and strong men in ancient Mesopotamia, which formed into a Christianity which made Eve the cause of the fall of man. Gender, however, in the West was a less hierarchical process. There was a matriarchy at one point for the Pueblos in the Southwest in Mesa Verde according to “A Pueblo Social History” by John Ware, which shows that the Pueblo society was predominantly matrilocal, and matrilineal, meaning the women would own the fields and the house, and the men would take care of different tasks. In the Hopewell there was a decentralized society with weakly institutionalized roles according to Christopher Carr’s “Gathering Hopewell,” which had gender variation on the record in the Shaman at the late Woodland period. There were likewise, many accounts of gender variation which were called “berdaches,” from Spanish colonizers which Roscoe describes in his monograph “Changing Ones.” People are multiple genders as well in the Arctic, and the account “The Many Faces of Gender” show people sometimes even becoming another gender to escape a ghost. But all of these practices, threatened by culture and time; things such as television show traditional western roles, which enculturate people into specific genders. Such as the continual creation of films that involve a man and a woman in a relationship, without any alternatively gendered characters. If there is a queer character, they may be a punchline, or a stereotypically sassy character. Sometimes movies and TV, unless they are shows like “Hazbin Hotel,” or “Stephen Universe,” don’t feature any queer characters. Some would argue Spongebob is a queer character, due to his lack of attention to what is considered manly, but queerness is never really explored very deeply in the original seasons of Spongebob. Even the notion of gender as tied up with biology is an outdated assumption. Biology is variable, and has people who have chromosomes that don’t match their gender assigned at birth, that may make someone have a body that does not match what typically is expected for certain bodies. This means people can be intersex, or they can have an assigned male or assigned female body that has parts that don’t match up to just xx or xy. This is aside from the fact that performances vary throughout the ages. In the 80s people like Prince, and Boy George were bending gender expression, and even in the 60s and 70s David Bowie was crossdressing and expressing himself in ways that were not usual for the assigned male at birth person at that time. There was also glam rock such as the New York Dolls, who work makeup and dresses as an expression of queer rebellion, when most of the genre was actually supposed to be coded as cisgendered and heterosexual. You could construct a whole wardrobe of basically what is considered a feminine outfit, constructed through clothing through history that is considered “for men.” So what does that mean? It means that there is no reason to say that one item of clothing is “for” one group, and “not for” another. Gender expression is a fungible signifier, meaning it is an expression that can be changed through time. Queerness as escape If fixed, binary gender, is what Max Stirner would call a “fixed idea,” then queerness is a rupture with the temporal flow of gender, into a multiplicity of expressions. Queerness is not in time the same way that gender is, queerness is a temporal instant in which change occurs, and the word queer also has the implication of unusual. Something which is unusual strikes you as uncanny, something which is familiar, and yet unfamiliar. Why do homophobic, transphobic, conservative people, usually online, react so negatively when confronted with the notion of queerness, seeing it, thinking about it, thinking it may apply to them? It’s because gender requires upholding an image when it is a fixed idea that is obeyed dogmatically, a fixed idea that makes people behave in a negative manner when what Lacan calls “the imago,” (Ecrit) is threatened, meaning the image of yourself. The transphobic person actually needs the trans person to uphold their imago, in the sense that without the trans person the insecurity would have nothing to uphold itself by saying what it is not. Bigoted cisgender, meaning gender assigned at birth identity, is parasitic on trans people, in that it needs them as a scapegoat to uphold its own rigid gender roles, but it also is not a symbiosis, but a parasitic relationship, because the bigot seeks to eliminate the trans person, either in expression or in life. Queerness is also a multiplicity of impulses beneath consciousness. It’s change itself, difference, multiplicity. Gender identity itself is part of an assemblage of social machines. Clothing companies, marketing techniques, family influence, friend circles, they all influence us, but we can choose to cut against the flow of time and make our own choices as to what we want our expression to be. There is no qualitative difference in abolishing essentialist notions of gender, while at the same time expressing yourself however you want. Abolishing gender essentialism is a matter of hierarchy, in a way, as even difference, and what Deleuze calls the rhizome can have hierarchy. There is hierarchy mixed in with everything we do, but there is also good and bad hierarchy. Gender essentialism is a micro fascism, meaning it is an intensity of restriction forcing people out of their own desiring machines. One’s own desiring machines are one’s own impulses, which are directed or repelled towards various social forces. Social machines interact with desiring machines as one and the same process of arrangement, otherwise known as assemblage. Micro fascism is an intensity of bad hierarchy, like queerphobia, Islamophobia, racism, etc. based on essentialist thinking. Desiring machines are the impulses, which themselves are infinitely multiple, and cut against against the flow of the fixed ideas of gender in time and consciousness. It is because of queerness that gender changes through time. Plato had what he calls the instant, which he calls a queer thing in the Parmenides. Identity and expression disconnected We’ve talked about how gender identity is a conscious phenomena, and queerness is a rupture with conscious identity, but further complicating the gender picture is the way that your identity can be one thing, but your expression could be an entirely different cultural expectation. David Hume had what is called the “is/ought” divide, but this is not because is and ought are separate. Facts and values can be looked at the same way as the identity and the expression. In the same way that facts and values are connected, gender and identity are connected. If you have a fact in one corner, it does not necessitate that there will be a corresponding value in another corner. For instance, if you’re a Catholic, that doesn’t mean that you won’t be a trans person. You could hold the facts of the Catholic Church, and still feel that you are trans, or even be trans and identify as a Republican. A great example of the disconnect between gender and identity is what is called a “femboy.” Femboys dress in feminine attire, deemed feminine by culture and the fashion industry. They can identify as a man, but their expression has nothing to do with their manliness sometimes. Everyone is a mixture of different expressions, so they may still have some expressions that are one expression or another. But this is another thing that should be avoided even, the idea that we have “male or female enculturation.” This is an argument that Trans Exclusionary Radical Feminists (TERF) use to try to say that if you were assigned male at birth you still act like a man because you have been taught to behave as a man. That assumes that all men are treated equal, or that all men identify with the label of man, and that this label of man would correspond with an identity and expression that is infinitely man, to the infinite exclusion of the woman. That is not true, just like facts and values, gender identity and gender expression are infinitely mixed. There’s an array of identities which we pass through through life, infinite of them which are related to all the past events that have happened before. All the different time periods and their genders have meaning that expresses itself in a warped, and reconfigured way in the assemblage of each generation’s machines. The eternal return and gender abolition Abolishing essentialist notions of gender is a societal wide task, and all the expressions that have ever happened recur through trends that take what happened in the past and make it new again. Time is cyclical, and while the heat death of the universe may still occur, in the representational, scientific sense of time, there is always an infinite recurrence of everything that has happened, happening again in the eternal return. Queerness is not inside or outside of our heads, it is in a singularity as Deleuze would say in Difference and Repetition. The singularity means that all things are happening in a virtual field of identities and arrays of past expression re-occurring through the instant, which is the moment of change in which everything happens. Gender is part of a colonial capture into an expression where infinitely variable expressions are attempted to segmented lines into a conveyor belt. Queerness is not necessarily a good, or bad thing, it is outside of conscious expressions and responsible for them all. Throughout time, the ways that people have expressed their gender has seen different levels of acceptance. The goal is not to be detached from all time, and try to exist in a fortress of a-temporality. We all have consciousness, unless we are in a coma or dead, that is inescapable. We will always have hierarchical thoughts mixed in with our rhizomatic, and variable lines of flight which evade capture into dominant structures of gender hegemony. But there is always the threat that if we are not careful about avoiding restructuring a new gender, instead of micro transsexuality, the full array of the expressions of the impulses, then we risk reinstituting forms of control over people’s gender again. articles.title: SLDSA Statement on DHS Cancelling ICE Warehouse Plans
articles.author: Democratic Socialists of Salt Lake
articles.content: This Week, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it is abandoning its intention to build a detention facility in a warehouse on Salt Lake City’s west side. This partial victory belongs not to politicians grandstanding in the courts but to the tireless mass organizing of Salt Lakers and working people nationwide. From the activists who showed up week after week to protest at the site of the planned concentration camp, to the citizens who put pressure on elected officials to get creative when opposing this facility, to the workers who refused to build DHS’s brutal machinery. While we are under no illusions that the abandonment of one cog in the mass deportation machine will end ICE terror, we nevertheless celebrate this as a win and commit ourselves to continuing the fight. We must work to abolish ICE and DHS altogether. This starts by forcing cities like Riverton to cut their 287(g) contracts, the current campaign by our Immigrant Solidarity Working Group. If you, like us, believe that the only way to grind the gears of deportation to a halt is to build working class power, we invite you to join Salt Lake DSA and organize with us. articles.title: Toward Simp Liberation?
articles.author: Evelina Johansson Wilén
articles.content: In late July, New York magazine’s Cut published Ezra Marcus’s “ Revenge of the Simps ,” the story of Nikita Tyukalo, a twenty-one-year-old Andrew Tate acolyte who built a webcam sex-trafficking operation out of luxury rentals in the Seattle suburbs. Astonishingly, Tyukalo was taken down by a community of self-described “simps,” obsessive online fans of the young women he exploited who noticed something was amiss while watching hour after hour of their streams. Tyukalo modeled his enterprise directly on Tate’s “Pimping Hoes Degree” course, which teaches men how to groom women into online sex work and confiscate their earnings. The men who worshipped his models from the other side of the screen, meanwhile, formed an amateur investigative unit called the White Knights, compiled evidence of abuse, and fed it to police until a SWAT team came through Tyukalo’s door in June. Jacobin editor Meagan Day spoke with Evelina Johansson Wilén, a regular Jacobin contributor and socialist feminist scholar from Sweden, about the article and the real-life events it depicts. In addition to writing on dating , romance , fertility , family , childcare , and women’s labor , Wilén has conducted research on incel communities and the sugar-dating industry. Day, meanwhile, has contributed articles about the Donald Trump–era gender wars , the manosphere , and offshoots like looksmaxxing . Day and Wilén discuss the many questions raised by the Cut story: the entrepreneurial core of the Tate phenomenon, the brutal hierarchy that red-pill ideology imposes on men as well as women, and the problems intrasexual status competition poses to the resurgent project of male domination. Meagan Day This story caught our attention at Jacobin partly because many of us didn’t realize that Andrew Tate isn’t just an ideological figure — he literally provides his followers with a blueprint for running a pimping operation. That’s alarming enough on its own, particularly given how massive his global audience is among young men in particular. But then to learn that twenty-one-year-olds are successfully implementing this blueprint to exploit girls their own age and younger is beyond shocking. So it bears some discussion. Can you give a quick explanation of the Tate phenomenon? Why is this guy so popular? Evelina Johansson Wilén The focus with Tate has mostly been on his sexist language, not on Tate as an entrepreneur and mentor to other aspiring entrepreneurs. I think that’s a mistake, because people aren’t drawn to him only because they agree with his ideas about women. They’re drawn to him because he embodies a possibility of success, of rising and becoming something else. If you look at Tate’s movement not only as an ideology of misogyny but also of male self-improvement, it makes much more sense. Social mobility has stalled; wages are stagnant. The sentiments of meaninglessness and blocked mobility that Tate speaks to are real. The ideological move is to redirect those sentiments away from an analysis of social relations, and toward hating women and hating weakness in general. Tate even has, for example, a truly intense hatred of people who are gluten intolerant. And this is where his worldview simply reinforces capitalist ideology. You are self-made; you can never blame anyone or anything for your lack of success. Likewise, your gluten intolerance is just a question of attitude. You’re passive, you don’t really want it enough, and this is why you suffer. But what’s interesting about this article is that it suggests fractures in the picture. We tend to talk about the manosphere as one totality — the incels, the looksmaxxers, Andrew Tate, all part of the same awful phenomenon. But I think Tate’s intense hatred of weakness actually creates a real difficulty for men like the simps and incels, who are in many respects self-defined by their weakness or suffering or unmet desire. Meagan Day Tateism taps into a fear among young men that the world is strictly bifurcated into male winners and male losers. You see this among incels too — they believe it just as much as Tate does, the only difference being that they identify with the losers. Tate is not for incels; incels have essentially given up on joining the ranks of the Übermenschen . Tate is for the strivers, the men who believe that if they keep grinding, they can ascend. And the only way to ascend in this vision, or to validate yourself as a “high-value male,” is to establish an undeniable hierarchy over other people, to dominate and exploit them. Tate is living out the theory of male dominance, and the way that looks in practice is utterly sociopathic. Tate himself is probably a born sociopath. His most adept imitators, like Tyukalo, probably are too. But most of the young men interested in Tate’s ideas are not. They’re actively attempting to cultivate sociopathy in themselves, because they’re afraid that if they don’t, they’ll end up the losers of the intrasexual competition game. What’s fueling all of it is a mass panic that there is such a thing as an irredeemable loser guy, and each man’s private terror that it might be himself. Money is a major validator of male status, and so is control over women. Tate offers a blueprint for acquiring both. But ultimately those are means to an end. The linchpin of the whole thing is a cutthroat, zero-sum view of male worth. Evelina Johansson Wilén I agree, and it’s clearly a men’s game. The women in it have no real role except as tools. But here’s what’s interesting: within this game, Tate and his followers effectively tell the simps, “You are the real losers.” And when he pushes them down that deeply, it becomes impossible for them to relate to him. There’s a power struggle going on that breaks down any idea of a male collective. The competition is supposed to remain a competition among men, with women serving as simple currency. But push some men low enough and the whole structure stops working on them. In the case of the White Knights, they started identifying with the women instead. Meagan Day This article is the story of men who have essentially fallen into the loser male category — they literally spend all day chatting on a forum called SimpCity about their favorite porn streamers — and found a kind of redemption by disaffiliating from male exploitation. Sure, they’re mobilizing another male archetype familiar to patriarchy, the benevolent protector. But the article makes it clear they started to see these women as subjects with interior lives, began to genuinely worry about them, and were moved to intervene in their abuse. That’s what’s conjured in the article’s title, “Revenge of the Simps.” Tateism is built like a pyramid, with an apex-predator male at the top. That may work for the strivers who hope to climb the pyramid. But for the other men — the simps, the incels, the broke guys — it’s humiliating, and maybe the thrill of misogyny is not enough to buy them off. Evelina Johansson Wilén This is why I found the piece so interesting. When I was lurking on the incel forums about two years ago, the way they talked about Chads [superior, “alpha” males] was: Chads are, in a sense, stupid. They can’t see the world as it really is, but they’re winning anyway. The incels saw themselves as smarter, wiser, closer to the truth. That was their way of coping with failure. And that actually puts them in conflict with guys like Tate, who sees himself as a Chad. But in the forums I studied, the hatred was still directed almost entirely at women, and the solidarity was directed at other men in the same situation. What’s happening in this story is different, which makes me think something may be evolving. When I followed the incel community, there were constant internal debates. For instance, once they developed the idea of male victimhood, they started making distinctions: if you have mental health issues, if you’re black, if you’re poor, then your victimhood is greater. And others would push back: “We’re supposed to be a collective, and you’re wrecking it by ranking who’s most vulnerable.” My point is that these forums aren’t just people repeating an ideology at each other. There are real discussions going on, real evolutions taking place, and we need to acknowledge that even while maintaining that the main ideas they work from are awful. This is the first time I’ve seen a group connected to this incel-adjacent environment really fighting for the women against the Chads. That’s a notable development. Meagan Day The simps were already interested in cracking the case and protecting these women from the beginning, but their zeal was really inflamed by Tyukalo coming into their chat and denigrating them, calling them losers. He kept calling them the N-word, oddly, which I think was meant to communicate that they occupy the lowest rung of society and thus had no standing to criticize him. He mocked them, and it increased their appetite for revenge. And the form their revenge took was liberating these girls from his trafficking operation. Instead of mass paranoia about being a loser male — and hatred of women in particular for failing to rescue men from that status by sleeping with them and marrying them — maybe some of these men could get fed up and start to turn on the structures of male domination themselves, structures that are demeaning and humiliating to them personally as well as to women. I’m sure I sound too optimistic, but it’s at least a useful thought exercise to map the weak points in the ascendant misogynist ideology. Evelina Johansson Wilén There’s one moment in the article where one of the simps reflects on exactly this. He says, essentially: this is all part of a bigger structural phenomenon, and how have we been part of creating it? It was a beautiful moment. Meagan Day The simp speaks! He basically says that masculinity and femininity are in profound crisis, and that being a simp is the outcome of those crises for him, and simphood puts him face to face with the struggle not to become what he despises. It’s genuinely moving. Evelina Johansson Wilén As you said, maybe we’re being too positive. But in one sense it would be surprising if this didn’t happen. In Tate’s world, not everyone can ascend. Contrast that with Jordan Peterson: whatever else you say about his ideology, there’s nothing in it that structurally requires most men to fail. With Tate, it’s total. Failure is not only assumed but required for most men. Meagan Day For there to be dominant men, there must be loser men. Tateism is not a politics of male solidarity. It relies on the continuation of mortal intrasexual combat. And the question becomes: How long can the men at the bottom be bought off with the promise that women, at least, are inferior to them? That’s the only deal on offer, and it may not be tolerable forever. Plus, men like Tate and Tyukalo may be the women’s pimps, but they’re also the simps’ drug dealers. These men are clearly addicted to porn, and their lives are no doubt suffering for it. It’s not just that the women are being exploited and the men are being humiliated; men’s porn addiction is being cultivated and mined for profit too. That should give them another incentive to break ranks. Many people will read this story as a sign of the apocalypse. We don’t want to paint too rosy a picture — there’s much to find disturbing. But what you and I are saying is that there’s a surprising little glimmer of hope in it. Evelina Johansson Wilén Maybe what we should be thinking about is not the revenge of the simps but the emancipation of the simps. Revenge keeps you inside the same frame of combative masculinity. Emancipation implies the beginning of something new. We don’t know if it will happen, but we can see how it might.
