articles.title: How China Picks Its Winners and Losers
articles.author: Daniel Cheng
articles.content: For those who went through the American education system, China’s National College Entrance Exam or gaokao may seem like a simple Chinese equivalent of the SAT. But the gaokao is vastly more important than any standardized test in the United States. College admissions in the United States are holistically determined, involving a consideration of a wide range of variables of which standardized tests are only one. For the vast majority of students in China, gaokao performance is the main factor determining whether they will be admitted to university. This grueling test helps decide the fate of millions every year. In The Highest Exam , Ruixue Jia and Hongbin Li show how the gaokao’s influence goes far beyond the education system. Jia and Li, who themselves took the gaokao, define the exam as the final showdown in a “centralized hierarchical tournament.” Every year, the gaokao is taken by over ten million high school students and repeat candidates. The student’s score doesn’t really matter; what does matter is their position relative to other students within their own province. The logic of the system is inherently zero-sum. One’s success is predicated on the failure of others. The stakes of this zero-sum tournament are extraordinarily high. In the United States, the importance of one’s undergraduate degree begins to fade into the background as one accumulates work experience or acquires a postgraduate degree. In China, a gaokao-determined undergraduate education will follow you for life. Doors leading to the best careers are permanently slammed shut if your gaokao score is too low. As Jia and Li point out, “attending an elite college affects your economic bracket for the rest of your life.” An Education Affordability Crisis The high stakes and extreme competition of the gaokao means there’s enormous pressure on parents to invest in the educational arms race. While Americans often lament the exorbitant cost of higher education, The Highest Exam shows that Chinese households also face massive education costs, just at different points in the system. China’s elementary and middle schools are free, but generally high school is not. Students and their families have to pay for tuition, uniforms, and sometimes room and board, which makes up the bulk of education expenses. In addition, expensive tutoring is a de facto necessity for urban students. Entry into the best elementary schools is determined by school district residency, although it is not unknown for wealthy parents to pay a large one-off fee or leverage special connections get their kids into the best schools, even though China’s ministry of education has repeatedly ordered localities to eliminate fees associated with admission. Buying an apartment to meet residency requirements is ludicrously expensive, with home prices in Beijing’s best school districts higher than even Palo Alto. In one section of the Highest Exam , Ruixue and Li report instances of parents paying entrance fees reaching as high as $75,000, over fourteen times the annual median disposable income in China. Only parents at the top of the socioeconomic pyramid have the connections to get their kids into these schools. Even with these incredible barriers to elementary school admissions, there are still more applicants than there are spots, meaning students have to take an elementary school entrance exam. To prepare for the exam, parents start their children on the tutoring grind as early as age four. These accumulating costs mean that families spend massive sums on putting their kids through school. Households with students spend an average of 17 percent of their household earnings on education. This financial burden falls much harder on lower-income families desperate to move up the socioeconomic ladder. Despite spending far less in absolute terms on education than rich families, households in the bottom quartile, who “only” average $1,280 a year, spend 57 percent of their household earnings on education. Even if the gaokao itself is the same for all students, the resources that families can bring to bear are not. The intense pressure of China’s education system and its early starting line have created a student mental health crisis impacting students as young as seven. The K-Shaped Labor Market Seen from another perspective, the existence of the gaokao within a nominally communist country is quite ironic. It replicates capitalism’s zero-sum competition between workers for jobs within the education system. Securing a spot in one of China’s best colleges means kicking other students down the ranking ladder. This means that from a very early age, the gaokao instills a gladiatorial mindset into Chinese students. Instead of promoting the warmth of collectivism, China’s education system incentivizes cold individualism. But when compared to the US system, China’s model appears less cruel than it does at first glance. Although rich Chinese families spend more money on their children than their poor counterparts, students from families in the top wealth quintile are only 2.3 times more likely to go to an elite college than those from the bottom quintile. In the United States, the wealthy are eleven times more likely to send their kids to the most prestigious universities. For all of its faults, a univariate standardized testing system is relatively more meritocratic and allows for higher social mobility. But social mobility is not the be-all and end-all. In a society characterised by massive inequalities, meritocracy more often serves as a system for legitimizing these disparities rather than correcting them. If exams are seen to be fair, then it is much harder to take issue with the winners and losers. What The Highest Exam implicitly reveals is that the gaokao is symptomatic of a deeper problem in China: the brutally competitive and highly unequal labor market. China’s youth unemployment rate is almost 18 percent , more than double the United States’. Within the People’s Republic there is intense competition for the best jobs, with 150 to 250 résumés per job opening in the most desirable sectors. Given the K-shaped dynamic at the top and sluggish-at-the-bottom nature of the economy of many advanced capitalist countries, not attaining a high-skilled job can often mean being thrust into the low-wage, long-hour world of gig work . The cushy government jobs allocated to top students are so desirable because they provide housing, education, and health care benefits that few others can access. The gaokao’s ruthless competition “succeeds” in preparing Chinese students for life precisely because this competition matches the post-college winner-takes-all nature of the capitalist economy. Thus, the real solution to the gaokao’s problems isn’t education reform, but dealing with the extreme inequality for which the test is just a sorting mechanism. If China became a more equal society with a progressive tax structure that invested in universal social services, much of the gaokao’s stress would disappear, as the stakes of the tournament would be vastly lower. A poor test score wouldn’t translate into lower wages, bad educational opportunities, or a lack of health insurance. It would be much easier for families across the People’s Republic to slow down the race for educational arms proliferation. The perception of the gaokao’s meritocracy is in practice a barrier to a more egalitarian People’s Republic. China’s social institutions are notoriously corrupt and systematically favor the wealthy and well connected. As Yuen Yuen Ang has shown , bribing officials with “access money” is a key ingredient to business success. Because the gaokao is fairer than these institutions, the distribution of jobs and security that it produces is seen as justified. This has had effects on social attitudes in the country. Surveys show that most Chinese citizens believe that poverty is due to individual failings like laziness or lack of talent. Only 25 percent of survey respondents believed there should be redistribution from the rich to the poor. If the gaokao tournament is fair, then its losers are seen as deserving of their suffering. All of this means that the gaokao’s problems lie in the deeper ills of China’s political economy. The challenges posed by a highly bifurcated K-shaped economy cannot be easily solved by educational reform. Given China’s current economic trajectory, students and parents have little cause for optimism.

articles.title: The Elisions of American Realism
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Jean Allen A few weeks ago on Chapo Trap House (#1051), the hosts interviewed Tim from the podcast All Lawyers Are Bastards , and his conclusion was notable in how often I’ve heard permutations of it: “It’s very hard for me to envision right now without a really severe legislative reform, a Congress in the next 8 to 10 years that’s really capable of doing anything of note, right? And that’s one of the ways the Supreme Court’s able to kind of create this space for themselves is they just kick things over to Congress and say, ‘it’s Congress’ responsibility to do this, not us, right?’ And so that’s when they decide not to act. But that does mean that Congress is probably not going to be able to create new federal legislation that carves themselves out a unique role, right? And if they do that, they’re probably not going to be able to effectively craft legislation that actually curtails those rights. So I think working in local municipalities and states can be one area where I think you can see a little more change.” This is the logic that I have seen consistently throughout my life (that it is not realistic for any systemic change to happen), but it is rare to see it all laid out like this. My parents’ generation loved the bumper sticker slogan – “think global, act local.” Yes there are big global problems that we are increasingly connected to, but really, you have the most power locally. Like everything in our postmodern world, this is a strategy that is always new, always obvious, but it can never be said to have been tried and failed. By my sister’s apartment there is a dangerous intersection. After almost a decade of organizing, it finally has a stop sign. That is the “stuff” you get done at the local level if your goals are in any way opposed or even orthogonal to capital. I know people who have spent their whole political lives defending a few acres of wetlands, or trying to get speed bumps installed on one residential street, or trying to get the police of a village to be marginally more accountable. Meanwhile, Elon Musk has made 998 billion dollars, reactionary politics have been on the rise everywhere, hot wars are returning to global life, and the world seems destined to careen towards an unmanageable level of heating. “Act locally” has failed as a project. I do not mean to diminish this kind of work. “Act locally” is a truism for a reason. But I want to focus on the elision here. An elision is a linguistic term for the omission of a syllable in speech, like saying you’re ‘gonna’ instead of ‘going to’. There is an elision between ‘think global’ and ‘act local’ – don’t waste your time on any kind of big demands. We are totally, abjectly powerless at the systemic level. In Rochester a 75-25 vote in support of the Police Accountability Board in our 2019 referendum has been eaten, slowly, by the court system. A half decade earlier, the insurgent mayorship of Chokwe Lumumba in Jackson, MI, tried to raise local minimum wages, only to have that power stripped from him by the state legislature. Any success at any point within our system requires the acceptance of the whole rest of it, requires super-majorities and the base for sustained legal fights; because the government that we have been taught is meant to serve us , is actually tremendously stacked against the empowerment of the working class. That system has not served any of us in the whole of our political adulthoods. And just as ‘Capitalist Realism’ accepts that “it is easier to imagine an end to the world than an end to capitalism”, there is an American Realism which accepts, to a greater or lesser degree, the perfection/permanence of the US constitution, and restricts its political project to fit itself within the disciplinary grounds of that system. I said this in June’s newsletter reviewing a folk album: ‘domination has a blast radius’. Constantly elliding over our total powerlessness at the level of the system is bad for us. Watching 17 years of protest movements be responded to with total indifference from the government which ‘serves us’ is not just a rational problem – it’s something that fucks up our ability to feel empowered in the rest of our lives. That’s to say nothing for the twisted kind of person who really gets into this. There is a kind of attitude developed within our schools and ‘intelligencia’ which says: any call for systemic change, any focus on how unrepresentative our government is, can be seen as the product of a lack of civics education . This person has come to love our system, which gives so many opportunities to explain the suffering it doles out, because obviously anyone with an issue simply does not have enough education to know that their suffering is actually justifiable, is actually fine. There is a popular tendency on the left right now that holds that this is only a problem of will – that if we win hard enough, this all goes away. To that perspective this is all nonsense, since nobody cares about our system of government anyways. I get this perspective, but even while we fight for bread and butter demands, I think it’s important that we say the thing the rest of our political punditry, including many of our comrades, elide: “The government we have been taught is meant to serve us, actually disempowers working-class people, and that is wrong, and the world does not have to be this way.” This is argued in DSA’s new program , which says our enemy is “not just this or that cop, judge, or president, but the entire anti-democratic structure of our society. We are workers fighting to transform society: to win the battle for democracy, draft a new constitution, and create a democratic socialist republic.” I think this is important, because the first part of empowering ourselves is recognizing that we have been disempowered, and training ourselves to see the disempowerment of ourselves and our fellow workers as a moral outrage rather than something to be ideologically explained. Because at the end of the conversation the Chapos had with Tim, Will spelled out what this perspective really means: “[The] best you can hope for [is the] complete collapse of the United States, both as a government, and a country. So maybe some sort of natural disaster, or [something].” It is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of America’s undemocratic institutions. But accepting these premises only leads to doomerism, rather than action. In order to fight for stop signs, and speed bumps, and wetlands, we need to clear the anti-democratic road blocks. The post The Elisions of American Realism first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: Defending Indians’ Most Basic Rights
articles.author: Achin Vanaik
articles.content: With the global rise of right-wing and far-right political forces even in countries deemed democracies, civil liberties groups are under pressure as never before. This is certainly true in India, though the success of the latest spontaneous youth upsurge, under the banner of the ironically named Cockroach Janata Party, got international headlines and provided welcome breathing space. The protests emerged against severe educational manipulation, which damaged students’ future employment prospects. Some leaders from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) had to, politically speaking, tread carefully since a very substantial section of these protesting youths came from pro-BJP families. That didn’t stop BJP leaders from claiming that this movement was being manipulated by anti-national elements and groups, meaning, the more left-wing student participants and members of civil liberties groups in Delhi and elsewhere in India expressing solidarity and support. Had this movement not succeeded in achieving its key demand for official accountability, with the resignation of the education minister in late July, there is little doubt that the supposed anti-nationals would have suffered serious retribution. This is what makes a new book-length study by Ankita Pandey about India’s civil liberties groups (CLGs) so timely. She has given us the most comprehensive and sustained study so far of these bodies that are not controlled by political parties or state authorities at either provincial or central levels. Just as the historical evolution of civil liberties activism in the United States (shaped undoubtedly by various progressive social movements and struggles) has given its CLGs a particular character, this is also the case when it comes to grasping the nature of CLGs in postindependence India. Ally activism, or allyship, is a concept that has been around for perhaps more than two decades in the West but has rarely been used in Indian social science studies. It is not a term familiar to Indian civil liberties activists. The minimal, consensual understanding of its meaning is that it refers to the activism of relatively advantaged groups, who act together with disadvantaged/marginalized sections of society but have no “direct, personal or material stake in the cause.” This is accurate enough as a formal description of civil liberties activism in India. But a distinctive aspect is that the initiators and organizers of India’s CLGs have mainly been either self-conscious Marxists influenced by different Maoist parties and sects outside of parliament, or self-described moderate socialists. These latter have been inspired by the Gandhian tradition or by the anti-party vision of onetime communist M. N. Roy, whose Radical Humanism prioritized individual freedom, reason, and decentralized forms of democratic power and rule. The particular manner in which Pandey has developed and applied the notion of a “politics of amplification” reflects this reality. Unlike charities and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), Indian CLGs are not simple service providers regularly beholden to particular (often foreign) funders having their own biases and concerned not to ruffle the feathers of the powers that be. As self-financing voluntary organizations, CLGs could be said to have greater political autonomy and generally lean more to the left than their counterparts in other countries like the United States. They are unlike social movements whose leaders represent a particular social category and that must mobilize en masse to get what they want — the greater the numbers and the longer the duration, the better! The politics of amplification is very different from the “politics of representation” and direct struggle. As Pandey rightly puts it, “Allyship mobilizes credibility, not numbers.” However, the ideological alignments of Indian CLGs do affect the way they solidarize with or relate to the oppressed and their concerns. They make them perhaps more forthright in voicing their demands on behalf of, and not just at the behest of, those who are victimized. Indian CLGs forge temporary alliances with social movements and operate over a much wider range of issues because they are event-based responses opposing different forms of state repression. Yet they have also responded to intrasociety iniquities like communal violence and atrocities perpetrated in the course of land grabbing by big landlords. Composition, Origin, Variation The regional and national incarnations of Indian CLGs really emerged in the late 1960s and ’70s. The member-activists of the earlier two regional CLGs in the states of West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh were, in large measure, radicalized youth who strongly identified with the Naxalite struggle on behalf of the rural poor. They sought these activists’ release from incarceration and their rights to be treated by the state as political prisoners, not criminals. While Pandey’s book carries detailed accounts of state-level CLGs, the central focus, which also provides a template for wider overall judgements, is on two national-level bodies: the People’s Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) and the People’s Union of Democratic Rights (PUDR), both headquartered in Delhi. The author has widely interviewed their many participants and longtime members (these bodies were first formed in 1976) and deeply studied over 250 of their histories and reports. Key here is the period of Emergency Rule (from 1975–77): a watershed moment that exposed the fragility of India’s constitutional commitment to a liberal democratic polity, and which served as great fillip to the subsequent emergence of the PUCL and PUDR. Nested between the introduction and conclusion are five chapters that in turn explore and assess a) the membership and political trajectories of CLGs; b) how they relate to political parties; c) their operating methods and key functions; d) ideological debates within and among CLGs shaping their basic practice; and e) how as one particular embodied form of “concerned citizenship” (there are others like charities, resident welfare associations, and NGOs) they contested the state on behalf of civil society. Who are the CLGs’ members? They mostly come from middle-class, “respectable” professions like lawyers, academics, journalists, social workers, occasional celebrities from the arts and entertainment domains, and so on. This itself lends a certain respectability to the wider public concerning their interventions. Long-standing CLGs, like some regional ones, and certainly the PUCL and PUDR, have a steadier and more regular set of activists than those one-off groups that periodically spring up in response to some dramatic turn of events, do their reports, and then fade away. These actions, too, are testimony to the existence of a wider pantheon of the politics of amplification. Prominent scholars have characterized these CLGs as “non-party political formations,” an understanding that Pandey has rightly criticized as ignoring the more complex relationship between them and political parties. A number of party loyalists (a spectrum that includes left and far-left sects and both Indian National Congress and non-Congress oppositionists but excludes the culturally exclusivist BJP) were accepted as active members of CLGs. But for the most part, they were procedurally and numerically constrained from being able to turn them into party fronts. Fact-Finding Virtues and a Key Difference Fact-finding missions have been a central form of activity undertaken by CLGs. To retain their credibility, these reports — for example on unjustified police violence in Kashmir province — have had to imitate juridical processes of showing impartiality in the accumulation of material evidence, including witness recollections. Their aim is to expose deficiencies and possible cover-ups in official judgments and claims. This also allows a place for help from sympathizers both within and outside the ruling parties at local, state, and central levels. Mainstream media have often focused on the outcomes of such fact-finding reports, either to malign or endorse them in some measure. But beyond that, such missions have helped to legitimize the testimonials of ordinary citizens, ignored by an officialdom whose upper-class and caste ties motivate it to repress the truth. CLGs’ work has also been significantly helped by the establishment, after the Emergency period, of Public Interest Litigation (PIL). Through it, ordinary citizens and citizen groups have the standing to approach the High Court and the Supreme Court on behalf of the indigent and deprived to call for investigations and judgments alternative to otherwise official or dominant narratives. Given this “judicialization” of civil liberties activism, it is hardly surprising that some dedicated lawyers do pro bono work for CLGs and are a key component of such allyship activism. This legalism of both procedure and practice is common to all such groups. Still, there remains an important ideological difference between the PUCL and PUDR (as well as between and, to some extent, within other groups), not only at the level of motivation but also in their basic political and advocacy thrusts. In practice, the more moderate liberal-left wing of legalism aims to get state power to behave as the existing liberal democratic constitution at its best demands. The more radical left wing seeks to create a broader counternarrative, or what Pandey calls “discursive contestation,” to persuade the public to think beyond the constitution about the need for a more “revolutionary transformation” of the social order. Not surprisingly, the former is less prone to rationalize and in part justify the resort to violence by the oppressed or by their agents (far-left groups) to counter overt or more “institutionalized” forms of violence by social oppressors or the state. This may be the case even if this rationale is not explicitly declared by the CLG in question. To put it another way, the general literature on rights discourse has four major areas of debate: 1) the material and moral foundation for the construction of rights: universalism versus cultural relativism; 2) individual versus group rights; 3) the question of civic and political rights versus economic and social rights: Isn’t the sufficient and equal fulfillment of basic needs as important, if not more so, than equality of basic liberties?; and 4) how far to expand the domain of rights. It is really with respect to the last two areas that differences exist, deep down, between the two currents of activism, even when they are not perceived as such. The Concerned Citizen Under Fire In her penultimate chapter, Pandey refers to the “concerned citizenship” embodied by CLGs. Her book deserves much praise for the new ground covered and will instill in the reader greater respect and understanding for the role that particular forms of allyship play in the defense of democratic rights and in their extension to those in India most deprived of these rights. After her book was published, one more recent development has surfaced that obviously could not be featured in her text. It threatens to greatly accelerate the already ongoing erosion of democratic freedoms. For Narendra Modi’s government has declared that there is no single document or set of documents that axiomatically and irrefutably identify one as an Indian citizen. Even the passport will not do. In today’s world, to be a rights-bearing person you have to be a citizen. Only then can one avail oneself of the range of rights whose depth and scale varies according to the country to which one belongs. But what becomes of the capacities to exercise positive forms of “concerned citizenship” such as civil liberties activism, when the government has the arbitrary power to question and decide one’s very status as a citizen? So far, there has been no judicial rejection of this official presumption. It is uncertain that this will indeed happen. Now more than ever, parties, movements and CLGs need to fight together against this Hindutva-ized and thus truly anti-national government.

articles.title: Immanuel Wallerstein Predicted the Fall of the US Empire
articles.author: Gregory P. Williams
articles.content: In July 2002, Immanuel Wallerstein appeared on C-SPAN’s morning call-in program . He had just written an essay for Foreign Policy magazine with a provocative title: “The Eagle Has Crash Landed.” Wallerstein argued that the US position of dominance on the world stage was in decline. As he was speaking, less than a year had passed since the terrorist attacks of 9/11 and the subsequent US invasion of Afghanistan. The Bush administration was preparing its military and the American public for the invasion of Iraq that would begin in March 2003. George W. Bush, it should be remembered, was a popular figure at the time. The president’s approval rating hit a record 90 percent the previous September, and remained over 70 percent when Wallerstein went public with his message of decline. However, it must have seemed to Wallerstein precisely the right moment to intervene. He had written about US hegemonic decline since the early 1980s. Yet he still believed, in the moment between the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, that America had the opportunity to effectively manage its decline. Wallerstein did not think it was possible to extend a great power’s global dominance indefinitely. He saw that great powers become hegemonic — a term that refers to unmatched global dominance — due to economic, political, and military factors that also ultimately cause such hegemony to erode. US hegemonic decline began much earlier than 9/11, with the economic downturn of the 1970s and the American war in Vietnam. For Wallerstein, the United States faced the choice of all waning hegemonic powers: to decline gracefully or to decline precipitously. George W. Bush chose the latter. Today Donald Trump has further accelerated US decline by aggressively deploying one of the few weapons left for a dying hegemon: its extremely strong military. Cycles of Hegemony Why was US hegemony in decline? For Wallerstein, American hegemony of the twentieth century hardly differed from Dutch hegemony of the seventeenth century or British hegemony of the nineteenth. These three powers (and only these three, he thought) achieved hegemony by riding a wave of economic forces they could not quite control and by prevailing militarily over a rival. After triumphing, the hegemonic power went on to create organizations in its image. The British, for example, prevailed over France and then created the Concert of Europe in 1815. America’s rise to hegemony began following the global recession of 1873. As Wallerstein told the story, Great Britain’s declining share of world markets was due to the United States and its chief rival, Germany. The United States became a major producer of steel, then automobiles, whereas Germany became a major producer of industrial chemicals. Each state’s economic rise followed an internal political crisis and (relative) stabilization: for America, the Union victory in the Civil War; for Germany, unification under Prussian leadership after war with France. Wallerstein understood the two world wars to be an extended thirty years’ war between the rivals. He noted that the United Provinces of the Netherlands and Great Britain also became hegemonic following wars lasting about three decades (in the Dutch case, this came after the original Thirty Years’ War between 1618 and 1648). After prevailing over Germany and the Axis powers in 1945, US leaders believed that it needed three things to maintain its prosperity: one, international customers for its industrial production; two, a world order guaranteeing commerce at a low cost; and three, a compact of sorts ensuring that production would be unimpeded. Washington achieved these objectives by reconstructing Western Europe and Japan, by creating major international institutions such as the United Nations, and by striking a kind of bargain with the Soviet Union. The last of these moves, symbolized by the Yalta conference of February 1945, was for Wallerstein much more significant than the founding of the UN two months later. In the conventional view, the Cold War of roughly 1945 to 1991 (to use the longest possible measurement) was a contest between American and Soviet adversaries. For Wallerstein, this period was really structured around an implicit compact between the great powers. The American sphere of influence covered about two-thirds of the world, with the Soviet sphere of influence accounting for the rest. Each power could dominate its zone of influence and use the threat of the other to corral reticent partners. Yalta was enforced by a “balance of terror” between the nations. The peak of American hegemony ran approximately from 1945 to 1970. Like all hegemons, the US became a victim of its success. By 1970, Western Europe and Japan were in Wallerstein’s view the economic peers of the United States. In the process of building up trading partners, crucial to American postwar success, the US also built up rivals. Like all hegemons, the United States began to lose its economic advantage in the same sequence through which it was originally built. First, the hegemon loses its advantage in agriculture and industry. Then it loses an advantage in commerce. Finally, it loses its advantage in finance. Also in the 1970s, Washington’s defeat in Vietnam exposed US military weakness and showed its inability to impose its will on the world. Vietnam, Wallerstein wrote, symbolized a rejection of the US world order by the forgotten peoples of the world, sometimes called the Third World, sometimes called the Global South. The independence movement in Vietnam against colonial powers (France, Japan, and the United States) was an extension of the global protest movement that came to a head in 1968. According to Wallerstein, “the 1968ers did not merely condemn US hegemony. They condemned Soviet collusion with the US, they condemned Yalta,” and they saw only “two camps — the two superpowers and the rest of the world.” The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, again contrary to conventional wisdom, was for Wallerstein a disaster for the United States, because it lost its great Other. In a 1992 essay , Wallerstein insisted that the Cold War was “not a game to be won but rather a minuet to be danced . . . The end of the Cold War in effect eliminated the last major prop of the US hegemony and the US prosperity, the Soviet shield.” Washington’s response to hegemonic decline has been to assert its greatness, in speech and in deeds, seeking to reclaim its position in the world. But, as Wallerstein explained on C-SPAN, “if you’re number one, you don’t have to shout that you’re number one. People know that you’re number one. If you have to shout, there’s something wrong. There’s something going on.” Shooting the Messenger Many C-SPAN callers were not happy with Wallerstein’s message of decline. One asked if flags flew on the Yale campus, given Wallerstein’s apparent anti-American bias. Another accused Wallerstein of being a Vietnam draft dodger, without realizing Wallerstein had been drafted at an earlier stage during the Korean War. A third shivered at the thought of Wallerstein as president: “If a guy like him were to be running the United States, the United States would end up like an armadillo, rolled up in a ball, waiting to be kicked.” Such expressions of outrage were normal for Wallerstein, who had written about the national-psychological toll that hegemonic decline takes upon those who experience it. It was a potentially dangerous period for domestic politics and the leaders to whom the public might turn. On the show, Wallerstein explained he was just the messenger, and that the United States was isolating itself from the world — not simply from nations it needed to court but from its closest allies too. “If you overestimate your power, and you go around acting like a bully,” he said, “you lose more than if you engage in elementary dialogue.” Some callers saw Wallerstein as being engaged in an attempt to reform US foreign policy. One asked how to respond to accusations of anti-Americanism. Wallerstein explained that he tried using reason. He argued that US foreign policy operated against individual interests: I’m not appealing to your altruism. I’m appealing to your selfishness. You are bringing about a much swifter negative impact on the US and the lives you live. In terms of your own standard of living, in terms of your risk of death, in terms of everything that you stand for, you’ll be worse off pursuing these policies than if you shift policies. Decline did not mean catastrophe. Historically, hegemonic powers do not fall very far. They land among the other great powers, albeit with greater material comfort than most (just look at the Netherlands or the United Kingdom today). Furthermore, as Wallerstein wrote in that 1992 essay, decline could be “the greatest blessing of all.” The United States had an opportunity to embrace morality. It “was Abraham Lincoln who sounded the moral note: ‘As I would not be a slave, so I would not be a master.’” In the early 1990s, Wallerstein saw two possible futures for America. One would involve neofascism, characterized by social conflict, with the lower strata subject to brutality and prejudice. The second, more hopeful scenario would be a form of national solidarity through social democracy and the movement toward egalitarianism. Although Wallerstein was not prone to overly optimistic predictions, he thought the egalitarian path was more likely than the neofascist path. He envisaged catharsis from “a shared social stress,” combined with American economic prosperity and popular notions of liberty, that would produce a movement against the major aspects of “unequal allocation”: gender, race and ethnicity, age, and class. He figured that the momentum of 1968, having disrupted American hegemony and dethroned the ideology of centrist liberalism , would lead to a mass movement for progress. Wallerstein also had history as his guide. In the first two instances of hegemony in the capitalist world-economy, Dutch and British, hegemonic decline was followed, eventually, by a movement toward welfare and equality. Why should the United States be so different? However, Wallerstein also left open the possibility of neofascism. If the end of the Cold War meant the end of US dominance over two-thirds of the world, then it also meant the end of centrist liberalism as a cultural guarantor of the capitalist world-economy. At least since the revolutions of 1848, centrist liberalism had been the gravitational force that kept the radical left and conservative right in check. Centrist liberalism promised the realization of democratic rights and economic well-being, not immediately for all peoples, but in a slow and orderly process to be managed by the state over generations. Centrist liberalism, as Wallerstein put it in his book The Modern World-System IV , was used by “the strong [to] temper the discontent of the weak.” Strong individuals tempered the discontent of weak masses, and strong states tempered the discontent of weak states. Yet the US economic advantage faltered as the Global South began to reject the Yalta power structure. After one of the main players, the Soviet Union, fell apart, the weak masses and states proved to be not so weak after all. In this situation, for Wallerstein, “conservatives would again become conservatives, and radicals, radicals. The centrist liberals did not disappear, but they were cut down in size.” The ideological possibilities were now endless. After the Cold War, Wallerstein saw great potential for American hegemonic decline to be accompanied by domestic economic redistribution. Ten years later, the radical movement had not materialized, while conservative hawks were firmly ensconced in power. They sought to flex military might because, in their thinking, “if Washington doesn’t exert its force, the United States will become increasingly marginalized.” But Wallerstein saw their actions having the opposite effect. Given the inevitability of decline, the muscular foreign policy of the Bush administration “will only contribute to the United States’ decline, transforming a gradual descent into a much more rapid and turbulent fall.” In retrospect, Wallerstein’s 2002 essay and television appearance constituted an attempt to move the United States off of its trajectory. He had evidently abandoned hope for a social democratic movement and now redirected his attention to the declining hegemonic power itself. In the summer of 2002, over six-in-ten Americans favored opening up a second war in Iraq. Wallerstein’s opinion was that of an unpopular but persistent group of critics. When faced with such criticism, President Bush would note simply note that history would judge his actions. Today it is clear that the hawks could not preserve American hegemony, nor remake the world in a manner more conducive to US interests. What has transpired between then and now? Decline and Denial The twenty-first century has not gone well for the United States. American leaders have pushed to reclaim lost hegemony. As US economic power has diminished in comparison to the rest of the world, Washington has used its military to demonstrate strength and to achieve policy ambitions. In fact, the United States has embarked on more military interventions since 1991 than it did between 1798 and 1990. This choice was the classic strategy of a declining hegemon in denial, aware of its descent, but unaware that its best viable option was the proper management of decline. The United States has not made the world more peaceful or more prosperous, nor has it improved the nations it invaded. In European Universalism: The Rhetoric of Power (2006), Wallerstein questioned the logic of interventionism. The invading power rarely makes the invaded place better off than if it had not intervened, a conclusion confirmed by US military adventures across the Middle East. Wallerstein’s 2002 verdict could have been written this year (or this week for that matter). He wrote that the United States finds itself “a lone superpower that lacks true power, a world leader nobody follows and few respect, and a nation drifting dangerously amidst a global chaos it cannot control.” The backlash of 1968ers that he described came from the nonaligned Global South as well as discontented masses at home. In the twenty-first century, the concatenation that began at the level of the world-system quickly moved to American domestic politics, and then outward again. The end of the Cold War unmoored radicalism and conservatism from centrist liberalism. The effects were drastic. Decades of neoliberal consensus were challenged by the likes of Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders. When Trump assumed the presidency — first in 2017, again in 2025 — he did so as a critic of America’s liberal order. However, “America first” has not resulted in the revival of domestic production, improved social welfare, or the protection of workers. Instead, Trumpism is characterized by massive, brazen corruption (at home and abroad), militarism abroad, and domestic policies of mass deportation. The United States has continued to expand its military commitments and military spending, but without a commitment to domestic social welfare. Meanwhile, optimism about the future among Americans has overall declined since 2013. In short, the United States has chosen the neofascist path that Wallerstein initially considered the least likely: social conflict, brutality, and prejudice. Members of the upper strata have sought to hold on to their remarkable privileges and rewards. Americans consequently have more precarious lives, living paycheck to paycheck , with fewer protections against the risks of illness, age, and employment instability. In 2026, America’s war in Iran encapsulates two tendencies of US hegemonic decline. One is the inability of the United States to get its way despite an extremely powerful military. The other is the discontent of the American public at a diminished standard of living and a leadership class it no longer trusts. Such feelings of discontent, as Wallerstein noted, can be powerful catalysts for political action. Washington may find itself surprised once again by chaotic global and domestic events it cannot control.

articles.title: Utopia Is a Promise Worth Fighting For
articles.author: Matt McManus
articles.content: The haunting impossibility of a society that lives up to our stated ideals can feel painful when set against the actual societies that fall so far short of them. This is why the dream of utopia, or “no place,” has disturbed the sleep of many thinkers for so long it can feel instead like a nightmare. Given the hypocrisy of a world where cruelty often feels like the point, what business do we have supposing things could be better? How can allegedly wise and intelligent people dream of utopia when wisdom and intelligence all point to its impossibility? David Albertson and Jason Blakely’s new book Utopia for Our Century: A Manifesto of Hope presents a thoughtful history of those daring souls who have dreamed of better. But more than a history, it attempts to think through the political and ideological value of utopian thinking and push against the line that it is just wishful thinking. Albertson and Blakely find much to admire in utopian authors, seeing them as “virtuoso dreamers, who lived realities at least as bleak and fearsome as our own but did so with indestructible hope.” At their best, utopians emphasized hope without guarantees — a wise position that carves a middle path between blind optimism and the resigned inertia of faux “realism.” Their archetype is Thomas More, whose Utopia , published in the sixteenth century, christened the concept. For Albertson and Blakely, More gives us insight into the personality of utopians. They are not the naive optimists of caricature. Far from an airy speculative thinker, More is one of the few major philosophers to have had a genuinely public political career, and during a singularly challenging period. He served as Lord Chancellor of England under the amoral and cruel Henry VIII. This was a tumultuous time for the country. Henry broke with Rome and declared himself head of the Church of England in order to annul his marriage and marry another woman. This produced major pushback, which Henry met with violent repression. That repression eventually caught up with More, a devout Catholic, who was put on trial for refusing to acknowledge Henry’s religious supremacy. More was unwavering in his convictions, leading to his execution in 1535. Albertson and Blakely understand that More’s tragic immersion in realpolitik is part of what inspired his turn to utopianism. His ironic designation of “utopia” as “no place” isn’t just intended to demonstrate the speculative quality of his thinking. More is drawing critical attention to the fact that no place on earth comes close to embodying justice, even though many ruling elites who have the power to change things claim to care deeply about being just. In a memorable passage, More describes a dialogue between Raphael Hythloday — the traveler to Utopia — and an unnamed lawyer. The lawyer claims to be concerned about law and order, and argues that the only way to preserve it is through brutal punishment. Hythloday notes that Utopia is a much safer place, in no small part because it is a far less unequal society where property is widely shared and there are few poor people. Moreover, their punishments for crimes like theft are far more lenient than in England, further expressing their humanist commitments. With “biting humor,” Hythloday observes that realists like the lawyer trap the poor in an impossible situation, “first making them into thieves and then punishing them for it.” Rather than undertaking reforms to achieve the greater peace and justice the lawyer claims to want and believe in, he doggedly doubles down on the “pipe dream” that “England could incarcerate and execute its way out of the problems of poverty (alas, the ruse still works like a charm).” In this sense, utopianism isn’t a fantasy about worlds that could never be, but a damning mirror that reflects how little we live up to principles we say we believe in. Moreover, by failing to commit themselves to justice in the name of “realism,” ruling elites are responsible for producing the very corruption they claim is the biggest barrier to doing better. More wanted to expose how this ideological attachment to the way things are, with all its flaws, was one of the major barriers to making things better. “More’s Utopia gradually submits his European contemporaries to the scrutiny of what if and its unmasking force,” as Albertson and Blakely put it. “Common attitudes of his day toward incarceration, private property, education, and medical care are exposed one by one as unworkable, unsustainable, and indeed unrealistic in light of Utopian achievements.” And yet, in just a handful of centuries, these all changed: “How many self-evident policies of More’s London have endured into our century, whether capital punishment for theft or the divine right of kings? The answer is clear: they have vanished.” Postmodernity; or, the Cultural Logic of Monstrous Utopias Contra our reputation for idealism, many of the sharpest left-wing thinkers have expressed deep skepticism about utopianism. This, of course, started with Karl Marx, who famously chastised socialists he disagreed with by disparaging them as “utopian.” In his more hard-edged moods, Marx mocked utopianism as writing recipe books for the cookshops of the future. Such schemes were nothing but a speculative and ahistorical indulgence (though one Marx himself often indulged in). Following in his footsteps, many orthodox Marxists insist socialism must be “scientific,” or it isn’t socialism at all. More thoughtful Marxists take a different approach. In his seminal Archaeologies of the Future , the late, great Fredric Jameson notes how utopian science fiction has often been a constructive genre for progressives to imagine what better futures might look like, the better to realize them. The genre, of course, began with More himself, whom Jameson describes as a broadly progressive satirist of power offering a damning “point by point commentary on English affairs and the English situation.” Utopian literature carried on in various forms as authors from Edward Bellamy to Ursula K. Le Guin used science fiction as a means of both criticizing the status quo and hypothesizing about what a better future might look like. But ultimately Jameson expresses wariness of the utopian genre’s transformative power and suggests it may well have been exhausted by the postmodern twenty-first century. He notes how today the utopian genre has all but evaporated, giving way to bleak depictions of the future where it is easier to imagine the end of the world than an end to capitalism. In a telling sign, even works that start by presenting utopias usually end by revealing them to be not all they’re cracked up to be. The seemingly idyllically pink world of Barbie (2023) turns out to be riven by suppressed existential dread and gender animosities. The more recent Star Trek series like Picard and Discovery take the bright cosmopolitan future promised by Gene Roddenberry’s United Federation of Planets and show that it has secretly depended on covert manipulation, exploitation of the marginalized, and much else. Contra Jameson, Albertson and Blakely see the utopian genre as very much alive but not well. This is a dire problem since the need for “constructive” utopias is urgent. Albertson and Blakely are very critical of right-wing populism and the havoc it is wreaking, but they argue that much of this flows from the Right’s own (frequently disavowed) utopian aspirations. These include the nationalist dream of a unified ethnos, which Albertson and Blakely describe as a “peculiar kind of failed utopia.” Nationalists conjure an “imagined spirit of the nation that creates an illusion of cultural unity” — one that purports to draw on real history even as they constantly downplay or militantly resist historical facts that don’t gel with the patriotic myths they want to spin. Albertson and Blakely wryly note that nationalists constantly have to “prop up the obvious falsehood that the make-believe geist [national spirit] remains pure from overlapping, constituent, or neighboring cultures, and that it never changes in time.” They also see many of the same fantasies at work in the Right’s “most feverish utopian hope”: that we might one day achieve the “most pristine, geometrical, frictionless vision of the ‘free market.’ Entire generations of Americans have lived as though the market were the only tolerable utopia.” Albertson and Blakely are scathingly critical of this vision, and rightly so, calling this a “monstrous utopia” for asking little of people and giving less in return, all while the money system is treated like a “minor deity.” I would go still further than Albertson and Blakely and suggest that the meritocratic conception of capitalism, that each will be rewarded according to what they deserve, is not just a bad utopian vision — it is the most pie-in-the-sky utopian vision ever conceived. Ancient philosophers had the wisdom to accept that only the very visible and omniscient hand of God could reward people based on what they deserved, and then only in a perfect realm beyond this one. Only American conservatives have ever imagined a world so fantastic that the invisible and mindless hand of the market would reward people based on what they deserved, and in this life. Compared to meritocratic capitalism, even the most rosy-eyed communist is a clear-eyed realist, since they only imagined it was possible to give people what they needed while keeping it an open question what they deserved. Is Utopia Possible Today? By contrast, Albertson and Blakely are more sympathetic to utopias on the Left but think they remain constrained by certain fundamental limitations. They express some sympathy for liberalism, while highlighting how “postwar liberalism stalled” due to a regression into “right libertarianism, sometimes called neoliberalism.” This regression into neoliberalism “betrayed the [liberal] tradition’s original ideals” of achieving liberty, equality, and solidarity for all. Albertson and Blakely are also critical of the Marxist tradition for failing to recognize how true revolutions never start in the economic sphere. Instead we need a transition in values by aiming for higher ethical standards. They don’t spell out what this would entail in detail, but their approving references to humanist and left-wing Christians like More himself, Martin Luther King Jr, and the late Alasdair MacIntyre provide many clues. What makes Albertson and Blakely’s position interesting is the extent to which they call for a utopian vision that will be at once liberal, anti-capitalist, and deeply spiritual. Needless to say, this is a challenging combination to achieve — though one might ask what good is an unambitious utopian vision? Unfortunately, the authors don’t make much of an attempt to spell this out in any kind of detail, even if they provide a suite of moving examples in the lives of More and King. My own Marxist instincts kick in here, leading me to suspect that individual acts of grace simply will not be enough. The lack of a clear theory of power — something to complement the fiery condemnations of injustice and the critique of ideological straitjackets — is a real limitation to their vision. But for all that, Albertson and Blakely are to be commended for the strength and boldness of their vision, even their audacity. They are no doubt right that a kind of utopianism may well be more realistic than a thoughtless adherence to a status quo that isn’t working. Doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results isn’t wisdom, after all. It’s insanity.

articles.title: The Roots of Capitalism: Slavery and the Sugar Trade
articles.content: The Roots of Capitalism is the first text in Studies on Historical Materialism, a new series from Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research. This series interrogates the pasts of the modern world from the standpoint of historical materialism – a method that explains history through material conditions and class struggle but insists that the dialectic between imperialism and anti-colonial struggles is central to how the modern world is made. Foreword Vijay Prashad There is a certain comfort in the stories that empires tell about themselves. These are stories of ingenuity, of discovery, of the steady march of reason and science. In these stories, capitalism appears almost as an inevitability, the natural flowering of human progress in Western Europe, propelled by technological innovation and the so-called Enlightenment. What these narratives leave out is not incidental but foundational: the violence that made the modern world. Prabir Purkayastha’s The Roots of Capitalism: Slavery and the Sugar Trade is an intervention into this cultivated amnesia. It insists that we look directly at the historical record and recognise that capitalism did not emerge from the gentle unfolding of markets and machines but from the brutal reorganisation of the world through conquest, enslavement, and extraction. Much of this study was written during Prabir Purkayastha’s 225-day incarceration in Rohini Central Jail in Delhi, India, on scraps of paper passed back and forth and discussed with those of us who visited him. It compels us to reconsider what we mean when we speak of the origins of capitalism and to ask: whose history is being told, whose suffering is being obscured, and what was the cost? At the heart of this study is sugar, not just as a commodity but as a social relation. Sugar was among the first truly global commodities, binding together continents in circuits of production, exchange, and finance. Its cultivation required vast tracts of land – seized through genocide in the Americas – and immense quantities of labour, supplied through the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans. Sugar, in this sense, was not simply produced; it was made possible through a system that treated human beings themselves as commodities. What Purkayastha demonstrates with clarity is that the plantation was not an archaic or pre-capitalist institution. On the contrary, it was one of the earliest sites of modern capitalist organisation. Here we see the integration of agriculture and industry, the careful accounting of costs and returns, the calculation of labour productivity, and the ruthless logic of replacement. Enslaved people were reduced to units of capital, their lives measured against their market price. The plantation, as Sidney Mintz observed, was both field and factory. The immense profits generated by slavery and plantation agriculture were not peripheral to European development; they were central to it. Sugar production, the trade in enslaved people, and the associated industries (shipping, insurance, refining, and finance) formed an interconnected system that fuelled capital accumulation on a global scale. The wealth generated in the Caribbean and the Americas flowed into European cities, underwriting the growth of industries and financial institutions. The sugar refineries of London, Bristol, and Liverpool were among the earliest industrial workplaces. They processed the raw sugar produced by enslaved labour, transforming it into commodities for mass consumption and for re-export across the globe. To speak of capitalism without speaking of slavery is therefore to tell only half the story. It is to accept a narrative that sanitises the past and obscures the structural violence upon which the modern world was built. Purkayastha’s work aligns with a long tradition of radical scholarship, from Eric Williams to Walter Rodney, that has sought to restore this missing history. But it also advances the discussion by focusing closely on sugar as a lens through which to understand the broader dynamics of capitalist development. What emerges is a picture of capitalism not merely as an economic system but as a global project of domination that involved the reorganisation of land, labour, and resources across continents; the destruction of existing societies; and the creation of new hierarchies of race and power. The interdependence of sugar and enslaved people as commodities illustrates this vividly: one cannot be understood without the other. This history is not merely of academic interest. The legacies of this system persist in the inequalities that structure our world today. The wealth accumulated through slavery and colonialism did not disappear; it was institutionalised in the financial systems, property relations, and global divisions of labour that continue to shape our present. To understand capitalism’s origins is therefore to better understand its contemporary forms and its enduring injustices. There is also, in this work, an implicit challenge to how we think about resistance. The system described here was sustained by violence, but it was also contested at every stage by the enslaved people 1 who resisted their bondage, by those who exposed the brutality of the trade, and by movements that sought to dismantle it. To recover this history is not only to confront the crimes of the past, but also to recognise the struggles that sought to overcome them. William Cowper’s satirical, anti-slavery poem ‘Pity for Poor Africans’ – printed and distributed in 1788 by the Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade and used as part of their campaign – begins with an unequivocal declaration: I own I am shock’d at the purchase of slaves, And fear those who buy them and sell them are knaves; What I hear of their hardships, their tortures, and groans, Is almost enough to draw pity from stones. I pity them greatly, but I must be mum, For how could we do without sugar and rum? Especially sugar, so needful we see; What, give up our desserts, our coffee, and tea? Besides, if we do, the French, Dutch, and Danes, Will heartily thank us, no doubt, for our pains: If we do not buy the poor creatures, they will, And tortures and groans will be multiplied still. The Conventional Narrative: An Overview The conventional explanation for the rise of the West – the lazy, Eurocentric account of civilisation – is that a few Western European countries came to dominate the world because of a set of events that took place only there. 2 According to this Eurocentric view, the key events of this period are the Age of Discovery (late fifteenth through seventeenth centuries), the Enlightenment (late seventeenth through eighteenth centuries), and the Industrial Revolution (mid-eighteenth through mid-nineteenth centuries). In this view, the Enlightenment accelerated scientific and technological development, helping to set in motion the first wave of industrialisation. The central impetus to progress in the West is thus framed as technological change, led by science and capitalist rationality, which shed the shackles of pre-capitalist production and created a new economic system based on ‘free’ labour. The role of the looting, genocide, and slavery that predated and accompanied the Industrial Revolution is airbrushed out of this history. 3 If mentioned, it appears at most as an unhappy adjunct or by-product of this history but by no means central to it. Factual history is quite unkind to this mythical explanation of the capitalist development of the West. The conventional narrative also airbrushes out three significant facts in the history of capitalism: first, that the plantation economy in the Caribbean and the continental Americas (both North and South) established sugar as a commodity of large-scale production and created a global market; second, that the foundations of British capital predated the Industrial Revolution; and third, that it was cotton, produced by enslaved Africans in the US South, that made the US a rising power and underwrote England’s textile revolution. 4 It is not our intention here to repeat what scholars such as Eric Williams, Walter Rodney, C. L. R. James, Joseph Inikori, and many others have already written about this issue. 5 In this study, we will focus on one crop (sugarcane) and its products (such as sugar, molasses, and rum) as commodities for the global market. Sugar was the first global commodity: it created the capitalist market and laid the foundations of the global financial system. It was accompanied by a second ‘commodity’: enslaved people captured in Africa and sold in the Caribbean and the Americas. The development of British, Dutch, and French capital, and later US capital, is as much the story of this vicious practice of treating human beings as commodities for the market as it is about the commodity produced through such labour. The dominant idea in Western scholarship and historiography about the modern world economy is that its foundations were laid by the Age of Discovery: the European ‘discovery’ of the so-called New World by figures such as Ferdinand Magellan (1480–1521) and Christopher Columbus (1451–1506) and the discovery of the sea route to Asia by Vasco da Gama (c. 1460–1524) when he sailed around Africa. The Age of Discovery is often linked with the Age of Enlightenment, despite the brutality of figures such as Columbus and da Gama. 6 Then, the story goes, the Scientific Revolution, accompanying the Enlightenment, led to the Industrial Revolution in Britain, followed rapidly by other parts of Western Europe. It was the transmission of the Industrial Revolution to the ‘New World’, primarily to North America – with the expansion of ‘free’ labour and the settler-colonial seizure of territory through genocide – that led the United States to become the leading economic power of the twentieth century. In other words, slavery, genocide, the expropriation of Indigenous peoples’ land, and colonial loot do not enter this sanitised picture of the development of capitalism except as minor aberrations. 7 How, then, was the supply of enslaved people from Africa ‘produced’? The starting point of the transatlantic trade is conventionally viewed as the time when Western merchants – the Portuguese, British, Dutch, and French – bought enslaved human beings in African ports. 8 Just as the genocide of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas and the Caribbean is covered up by the false narrative that their lands stood empty, waiting for the Europeans to come and claim them, a number of historians have argued that since slavery already existed in Africa, all the Europeans did was tap into the existing markets of enslaved people. 9 This account ignores the scale of the trade in enslaved people that the West introduced in Africa, which qualitatively transformed what was largely domestic slavery into an industrial-scale ‘production’ of enslaved people for plantations across the Atlantic. Claude Meillassoux describes this process as the production of enslaved people in the ‘womb of iron and gold’ – that is, through the gun-slave-money nexus, in which firearms and gunpowder were exchanged for enslaved people, whose sale generated profit. The ‘iron’ in this formulation refers to the use of firearms and gunpowder as trade goods exchanged for enslaved people and as instruments of capture, while the ‘gold’ refers to the money and profit generated by this trade. This is supported by trade records that show substantial exports of gunpowder from Europe to Africa during this period. 10 One result of this violence-driven trade, as with the genocide in the Americas, was demographic catastrophe. While the population in Asia and Europe grew by 300% or more from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century, in sharp contrast, the African population remained almost the same and in many regions declined. 11 This was a consequence of the violence wreaked on the existing social structures and the destruction of local economies through the forced capture and sale of human beings. The impact of slavery on the African population is often overlooked when considering only the number of enslaved people transported to the Americas and the Caribbean, which is estimated to be at least ten million. However, as Walter Rodney writes, this figure refers only to people who landed in the Americas and the Caribbean and fails to take into account the activities of the illegal slavers and the numbers of Africans who died crossing the Atlantic and during the process of their ‘acquisition’, or kidnapping, in their homelands. Taken together, these losses suggest that the total number of Africans seized for the transatlantic trade – including both those who survived to reach the Americas and those who died during capture, marches, detention, and the Middle Passage – was substantially higher, plausibly in the range of fourteen to twenty million. 12 It was not until the abolition of slavery that the continent’s population and economy began to recover, and more sustained growth did not occur until African countries achieved independence. This devastation in Africa was inseparable from the rise of sugar production on the enslaved-labour plantations of the Americas and the Caribbean. Traded on a global scale from the sixteenth century onwards, sugar underpinned the growth of European colonialism and the development of the global commodity market. In fact, it was to expand sugar production that the brutal and complex new system for acquiring and trading enslaved Africans came to be established, distinct from the pre-existing system consisting largely of domestic slavery. 13 Together, sugar and enslaved people became paired commodities, and the circuits of production, credit, and trade built around them helped lay the foundations of modern capitalism. This dynamic is especially clear in the Caribbean plantation complex, 14 which proved central to Britain’s capitalist development and forms one dimension of what Sven Beckert and Seth Rockman call ‘slavery’s capitalism’. 15 Riding on the back of the extremely profitable trade in enslaved people, the goods made from sugarcane (sugar, molasses, and rum) were among the first commodities produced for global markets. Before cotton production became the exemplar of both the Industrial Revolution and the horrors of slavery in the US South, sugar anchored a transatlantic system of labour extraction and exchange, linking plantation production to long-distance trade and re-export. From the sixteenth century until the abolition of slavery in the nineteenth century, sugar and its by-products circulated through interlocking markets, generating profits across shipping, insurance, warehousing, and finance as goods were exported, refined, and re-exported. The dominant narrative of triangular trade – the three-cornered exchange of enslaved people, raw materials, and manufactured goods among Europe, Africa, and the ‘New World’ – often overlooks other commodities essential to this system, including textiles and saltpetre (potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in gunpowder). 16 For example, through much of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries (1750–1850, according to Kazuo Kobayashi), textiles produced in India were shipped by the British and French East India Companies to the west coast of Africa, where they were exchanged for enslaved people. 17 Similarly, Europeans used saltpetre exported from India to manufacture gunpowder, which they then exchanged for enslaved Africans. In their assessments of the importance of the triangular trade, Ronald Findlay and Kazuo Kobayashi argue that in the third quarter of the eighteenth century, a significant percentage of British exports to Africa were re-exports from India, not European manufactured goods. 18 It was the colonial loot from India – land revenue extracted from the Indian peasantry – that paid for the ‘export’ of textiles and saltpetre from India. 19 Political economists like Adam Smith, for example, view this period either as mercantilist and, hence, inefficient, or as a source of originary accumulation – a precursor to the capitalist accumulation that followed. However, Marx makes it clear that this ‘so-called originary accumulation’ was expropriation, not accumulation. 20 It was loot, pure and simple, not savings or the accretion of a nest egg. In sugar production, slavery and its associated labour processes were a major source of both expropriation and capital accumulation. This form of capital accumulation rooted in the plantations laid the foundation for the Industrial Revolution. It is disingenuous to claim that the impact of colonialism on the colonies (in terms of deindustrialisation and the drain of wealth, for instance) was a separate phenomenon from the plantation economy based on enslaved labour and the broader ‘New World’ dynamic, or that these factors were not important in determining the development of capitalism in the mother country. Such a claim obscures the colonial foundations of modern capitalism. 21 Next, let us consider how the plantation system was developed to produce sugar, primarily by means of enslaved labour. This requires tracing the development of sugar cultivation and trade in the Mediterranean region as a precursor to the development of plantation-based production in the Atlantic world. How did the production, export, and re-export of sugar shape European finance capital and industrial development? Given that the production of sugar was founded on enslaved labour, to answer this question we must examine the dynamics of slavery and sugar production in the American-Caribbean sugar economy, with greater emphasis on the Caribbean plantation system under the Dutch, French, and British. This discussion illustrates that both sugar and enslaved Africans, produced and sold as market commodities, were crucial for early capitalism’s global expansion and production structures. Sugar Production in the Mediterranean: From Peasant Agriculture to Plantation Capitalism Before the Crusades, Western Europe (aside from its elite) was unfamiliar with sugar. 22 Then, two transformations occurred. First, the use of sugar, imported from the eastern Mediterranean, kept increasing, even after the Crusades failed to capture the ‘Holy Land’. Second, sugar cultivation spread westward from the eastern Mediterranean to the western Mediterranean and Iberia: first to Mediterranean islands such as Sicily, Cyprus, Rhodes, and Crete; then to parts of Iberia and North Africa; and later to Atlantic islands such as Madeira and the Canary Islands. This geography was shaped in part by climate: sugarcane requires a long, warm growing season and a cool but frost-free ripening and harvesting period. Frost can kill cane and damage its roots, which meant that cultivation was largely limited to the warmer Mediterranean, southern Iberian, North African, and Atlantic island zones rather than northern and much of western Europe. Unlike the peasant-based agriculture in the eastern and southern Mediterranean coastal plains, agriculture in Western Europe was based on a combination of peasant and corvée labour (unpaid labour that peasants were obliged to perform on land owned by the feudal manor, or demesne land). In the Mediterranean islands of Sicily, Cyprus, Rhodes, and Crete, settling or importing peasants from Italy or Greece was not a viable option because the Black Death (1347–1351) had drastically reduced the peasant labour supply in Europe and the Mediterranean. Instead, the West European rulers of these islands imported enslaved people from North Africa to substitute for the ‘free’ labour that corvée services provided in Western Europe. 23 This had enormous significance: sugar production morphed from the largely peasant-based production in the Arab world to the ‘modern’ slavery-based plantation economy in the Caribbean. Another important feature of plantations in the Mediterranean islands was the capital investment by big merchant families from Venice and Genoa: it was in these islands that the marriage of merchant capital and modern slavery began. Portugal extended this slavery-based sugar plantation model from the Atlantic islands closest to Iberia – Madeira, the Canary Islands, and the Azores – to Cape Verde, off the West African coast, and later to São Tomé, in the Gulf of Guinea (close to present-day Ghana). The final step in the transformation from peasant-based agriculture to the slavery-based sugar plantations took place in São Tomé. Plantation owners, generally from the aristocracy, got land from the Portuguese king, capital from Venice or Genoa, and enslaved people from Africa. The Portuguese transported this system to Brazil; from there, it spread to the Caribbean and later to parts of North America. Did these Mediterranean and Atlantic islands introduce any major technological change in the production of sugar? According to Ulbe Bosma, the answer is no. The earlier mistake that historians made was to obscure the technological similarity of milling and sugar-processing techniques across the eastern and western Mediterranean, Iberia, the Atlantic islands, and finally the ‘New World’. 24 In his extraordinary work The World of Sugar , Bosma summarises this journey: Sugar makers travelled from Egypt and Syria to Cyprus and Sicily, from where their knowledge and skills crossed into Valencia and reached Madeira. Portuguese sugar masters learned their art from the Muslims in Andalusia, who ruled it for 800 years, and brought it to Madeira and the Canary Islands. 25 The plantation model that would be transplanted across the Americas virtually unchanged, especially to Brazil and the Caribbean, began in São Tomé. The cane cultivated in the Americas and the Caribbean was from the Atlantic islands, where it had in turn been introduced from the Levant and Egypt. As for sugarcane cultivation, there were few major changes. The model continued to rely on the long-established technique of leaving part of the cane stalk in the soil after harvest so that it would produce a new crop (a process known as vegetative reproduction, or ‘ratooning’, that is still used today). Even as new crops were planted, shoots from the old stalks continued to grow. The Mediterranean islands remodelled the existing relationship between the peasant producers of sugarcane and those involved in the secondary and tertiary processes of crushing the cane, producing sugar from the juice, and trading the sugar. In the new plantation model, sugarcane production was integrated with the crushing, boiling, and refining processes at one site. This created the new ‘workflow’ of using enslaved labour all the way from the cultivation of sugarcane to the final product, whether as brown sugar or as crystalline white sugar, which was refined in Europe. Thus ran the flow on the sugar plantations: during the crushing season, the ripe cane had to be cut and crushed, and the juice had to be concentrated before it crystallised into sugar (see diagram 1). Once the juice was extracted by crushing the cane, it was boiled in a series of large vats or cauldrons that required a large amount of fuel to concentrate the juice into a thick syrup, which would then be cooled in inverted earthenware cones. This would enable its separation into sugar loaves and molasses. Processes of crystallisation, or further refining, were also adopted to produce sugar crystals rather than loaves. Diagram 1.
