articles.title: Chilean President Kast proposes constitutional reform to gain more powers
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Just as he promised during his election campaign, right-wing President José Antonio Kast has launched a series of reforms to radicalize the neoliberal agenda in Chile and intensify anti-immigration policies. However, one of Kast’s most important promises (which was a central pillar of his election campaign) was an ambitious legal reform to overhaul the law against organized crime. On August 17, Kast finally submitted his proposal to the Senate . Following the same model as other neoliberal Latin American governments that have reformed the law in recent years, Kast proposes that the “state of emergency” become a sort of political norm that can be used on a regular basis. During the 20th century, the Nazi philosopher Carl Schmitt had already stated that the sovereign is the one who can declare a state of emergency. For his part, the Italian philosopher Giorgio Agamben emphasized this idea but added that new governments were turning the state of emergency not into something exceptional, but into a routine tool of government used to control citizens and weaken democracies – a tool for which any justification, such as a “social threat,” is employed. Chile is all too familiar with how the power of force can destroy democratic processes (as demonstrated by the US-backed dictator Augusto Pinochet). Kast is attempting to formally align itself with this historical trend. To this end, in an apparent contradiction, he proposes reducing the state’s power to regulate the economy, while (according to the proposed law) strengthening its capabilities to prevent and prosecute crimes and “safeguard public order.” Chile’s former president, the center-left Gabriel Boric, said of Kast’s proposal : “It seeks to establish a state of siege for 240 days, with exclusive authority vested in the president of the Republic and an unprecedented restriction on freedoms never before seen in Chilean democracy.” He added : “Those of us in politics must be willing to collaborate with whoever is in government on matters of national policy, which does not mean compromising on our clear convictions.” What would change in Chile? Kast proposes eight specific constitutional amendments, along with 30 bills that, according to the government, are part of the Agenda Against Organized Crime and Terrorism (ACOT). The reform proposes that the president be able to declare a new type of state of emergency, which would be imposed by presidential decree in the event of a “serious and imminent threat to public safety or whenever public safety has been seriously compromised.” This state of emergency may be extended for 120 days by presidential decree, although further extensions would require the approval of the National Congress. In this regard, the president may “suspend or restrict personal liberty and freedom of movement, as well as the right to assembly; [and] restrict the exercise of the right to association; intercept, open, or search documents and all types of communications; and order the seizure of property.” According to Security Minister Martín Arrau, the introduction of a new type of state of emergency is justified to intervene in areas “where terrorist groups or organized crime operate and which are difficult to penetrate,” as reported by El País . Read more: Anti-government protests in Chile face heavy repression In areas declared to be in a state of emergency, the package of reforms and laws proposes that a general officer, appointed by the head of state, take command, although it is unclear whether this officer will be a civilian or a military or police officer. In addition, the package of laws proposes, as is the case in other countries, the creation of a registry of organized crime and terrorist organizations, against which the state must take action. Under the proposal, the president would have the authority to designate a particular organization as terrorist following a report from the Public Prosecutor’s Office or the National Security Council. It is important to note that the Executive Branch proposes withdrawing social benefits (such as health care) from those convicted of organized crime and terrorism, meaning these prisoners could be left without medical care. “When taxpayers fund benefits for people who have caused so much harm to society, there is a sense of injustice. That is what we want to correct,” said Arrau . Along these same lines, the reforms propose that a person convicted of these crimes be permanently barred from holding public office and be ineligible for alternative sentencing measures for 15 years. The Senate has 15 days to debate the proposal and render its verdict. This package of legislative reforms and far-reaching constitutional changes would set Chile on the path toward a security policy aligned with the model that Washington has been proposing for the past few years. Indeed, most governments aligned with the United States (in the coalition known as the Shield of the Americas) have replicated this model almost exactly.

articles.title: Israel escalates aggression in Gaza, Kushner returns to Washington empty-handed
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: At least 10 Palestinians were killed and 15 others were wounded in Israeli airstrikes that targeted the municipal police headquarters in the center of Gaza City and Nuseirat refugee camp in the middle of the Gaza Strip on Wednesday, August 20. Israel claimed that both assaults were launched to exterminate Hamas commanders and operatives. Nevertheless, Hamas rejected the allegations as “baseless and false,” accusing Israel of using such pretexts “to justify its aggression and cover up its deliberate targeting of civilian police and unarmed civilians.” The movement pointed out that the timing of the attack coincided with recent diplomatic efforts and meetings between mediators and US envoy Jared Kushner. This, in turn, “confirms endeavors by Netanyahu’s government to undermine stability efforts and reignite the war.” Wednesday’s massacre occurred one day after Israeli warplanes targeted a crowded café surrounded by displaced families at Gaza City’s harbor. The strike killed at least seven people, including a child, and wounded 16 others. The Israeli military used the same pretext to justify Tuesday’s deadly attack, saying it was targeting Hamas commanders, without providing evidence. Read more: Israeli airstrikes on Gaza beach kill dozens, including a journalist Kushner left the region without reaching a breakthrough in negotiations Both consecutive massacres were carried out right after Jared Kushner had held talks with Hamas’s political chief Khalil al-Haya in Egypt’s city of El Alamein on Sunday, August 16, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in Jerusalem on Monday, August 17. Kushner’s discussions with Hamas and Israel, however, ended without a breakthrough as both sides held their ground on core demands. Observers argue that Tel Aviv has resorted to escalating its aggression on Gaza and other parts of West Asia during the past three years, whenever US envoys arrived in the region to push negotiation efforts. Many believe that by derailing talks, Netanyahu ensures he stays in power for a longer period, especially as he faces corruption charges and fears that his party would lose its chance to win the upcoming election. Perpetuating the regional war and wreaking havoc in the occupied Palestinian territories in both Gaza and the West Bank in order to implement the “Greater Israel” project are apparently the only cards Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has left to remain in office. articles.title: Concerns over intimidation and lack of transparency loom over results of presidential race in Zambia
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Zambia has voted, and the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has declared incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema the winner of the August 13, 2026, presidential election. Running on the ticket of the United Party for National Development (UPND), Hichilema secured 2,965,326 votes, 60.49% of the 4,902,050 valid votes cast. His main challenger, Brian Mundubile of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), received 1,856,217 votes, or 37.87%. The result gives Hichilema a second five-year term. But the victory comes in a deeply contested political environment, marked by allegations of intimidation, arrests of opposition figures, political violence, disputes over electoral materials, a temporary suspension of vote counting, and growing questions about the transparency of the results-management process. Concerns grew when on August 19, reports emerged stating that former Zambian minister Mutotwe Kafwaya had been killed during a raid on Mundubile’s house. Socialist Party leader Fred M’membe described the killing as “very frightening” and “very saddening,” extending condolences to Kafwaya’s widow, children, family and friends. M’membe linked the incident to what he described as growing political divisions and intolerance in Zambia, warning that neither electoral disputes, political doctrine nor law enforcement could justify the physical elimination of citizens. “No crime can be committed in the name of elections or law enforcement,” he said, while paying tribute to Kafwaya’s memory and condemning the violence surrounding the country’s increasingly tense political environment. Read more: What’s behind Hichilema’s constitutional reforms in Zambia? Hichilema won decisively at the ballot box. Yet, the process has left large sections of the opposition questioning whether Zambia’s democratic institutions are still operating with the independence and credibility required. The major issues in the campaign ranged from unemployment and the rising cost of living, all while an unstable electricity supply continues to strain households and businesses. Fourteen presidential candidates Fourteen candidates contested the presidency. Alongside Hichilema and Mundubile, the field included Socialist Party leader Fred M’membe, Citizens First leader Harry Kalaba, Kelvin Fube Bwalya, Brian Mushimba, Given Katuta, and several others. Mundubile emerged as the principal challenger through an opposition alliance, campaigning on ending the prolonged load shedding that has crippled businesses and disrupted livelihoods, and on economic stabilization more broadly. A campaign marked by controversy The controversies did not begin on polling day. For much of the year, opposition parties complained of restrictions on political activity, arrests, and what they described as the use of state institutions to disadvantage political opponents. Among the most prominent cases was the arrest of Socialist Party president Fred M’membe on March 2, 2026 . M’membe was charged under Section 22(2)(a) and (b) of Zambia’s Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025, over remarks he had made publicly. The opposition also raised allegations of political violence during the campaign. On June 29, M’membe accused suspected UPND cadres of attacking Socialist Party members at a planned campaign rally in Kanyama’s Makeni Constituency. He alleged that three minibuses carrying suspected UPND supporters arrived armed with pangas and other weapons, assaulted party members, disrupted the gathering, injured several people, and stole a phone belonging to an SP parliamentary candidate. The Socialist Party also reported that one of its polling agents, Lovemore Chishimba, was killed on election day. The party has called for justice and says it remains committed to establishing accountability for his death. The Mundubile raid and questions over the electoral process Tensions escalated further when reports emerged that Brian Mundubile’s residence had been raided and several opposition figures arrested. Authorities described the arrests in security terms, accusing those detained of involvement in an alleged armed-insurrection plot, a characterization Mundubile has rejected. Perhaps the most consequential unresolved issue concerns the GEN 20 forms, the documents central to the presidential results-management process. Mundubile has demanded that the ECZ explain the custody and movement of the forms, questioning reports that they were collected from districts and raising concerns about possible interference or alteration. He has specifically called for clarification on who authorized the collection of the forms, the legal basis for moving them, and who had access to them. More broadly, the opposition is demanding independent verification and greater transparency in how electoral documents were handled. Harry Kalaba, who received 19,070 votes, described the campaign period as conducted under conditions of intimidation and irregularities, while also praising Zambian citizens for choosing peace over violence. But Kalaba warned that Zambia risked moving from being regarded as a model of democratic stability to becoming a cautionary tale. “The process we have just witnessed raises serious concerns that cannot be ignored,” he said. Reports of intimidation, interference with polling processes, inconsistencies in the handling of electoral materials, and uneven application of the law, he argued, pointed to a process that fell short of the democratic standards Zambia has historically upheld. As previously mentioned, reports emerged on August 19, indicating that a former Zambian minister had been killed during the raid, putting more scrutiny on the electoral process and harassment faced by candidates. Legitimacy question remains The election may have settled who will govern Zambia for the next five years. But it has not settled the question of how much trust Zambians can place in the institutions through which that government was elected. The coming months will reveal how the opposition’s complaints and concerns are handled and whether the reported political violence is investigated.

articles.title: Fidel Castro made Africa’s struggle his own
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: On August 13, 2026, the world marked one hundred years since the birth of Fidel Castro, the man who not only led the 1959 Cuban Revolution and the building of a socialist state, but also went on to become a key contributor in Africa’s twentieth-century liberation history. The centenary landed at a difficult moment for Cuba. An acute economic crisis, oil shortages, and a tightening US sanctions regime. But even under that weight, Cuba stands. And across Africa, Fidel is being remembered not as a distant Cold War figure but as a revolutionary internationalist whose name is stitched into the continent’s own liberation story. This legacy is well-deserved. Castro’s revolution triumphed in 1959, just as Africa was entering its most decisive decade of decolonization. At that point, only Ghana and Guinea stood as independent sub-Saharan states. Within ten years , the political map of the continent would be transformed. Cuba, a small island ninety miles from the United States, chose to see its own struggle as bound up with that continental awakening. Castro said as much in 1975, describing Cuba’s ancestry in Africa and the debt that history imposed; a promise, in his words. “African blood flows freely through our veins. Many of our ancestors came as slaves from Africa to this land. As slaves they struggled quite a great deal. They fought as members of the liberating army of Cuba. We are brothers and sisters of the people of Africa and we are ready to fight on their behalf.” What followed was six decades of doctors, teachers, soldiers, engineers, and political cadres sent to a continent thousands of kilometers from home. In an interview with Ignacio Ramonet , Fidel Castro reflected on Cuba’s commitments to other oppressed nations, including the struggles for independence across Africa. “Cuba’s heroic solidarity with our sisters’ nations in Africa has been well enough recognized. That glorious page of our revolutionary history deserves to be known, even if only to encourage the hundreds of thousands of women and men who are internationalist combatants, it should be written, as an example for present and future generations, nor, in my opinion, are people sufficiently knowledgeable about the history of Europe’s imperialist and neocolonial looting and pillaging of Africa, with, of course the full support of the united states and NATO.” Read more: Fidel Castro: a life of revolution Solidarity with Africa’s struggle for liberation Cuban doctors arrived in Algeria in 1963, an important detail that compliments the popular image of Cuban internationalism as primarily military-centered. From the beginning, Cuba’s engagement with Africa also involved medicine, education, and technical assistance. But the Congo crisis, and particularly the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, was a decisive moment in the development of Cuba’s revolutionary internationalism. Speaking at the United Nations in September 1960, Fidel Castro condemned the continued influence of colonial interests in the Congo and explicitly defended Lumumba. “The hand of the colonialist interest has been clear and visible in the Congo, and our opinion is consequently that colonialist interests have been favored and that every fact indicates that reason and the people of the Congo are on the side of the only leader who remained there to defend the interests of his country, and that leader is Lumumba.” Castro extended this argument to Algeria, where the struggle against French colonialism was still underway. Declaring Cuba’s support for Algerian independence, he challenged the claim that Algeria was an extension of France and condemned the violence being inflicted on Algerian communities. He contrasted the international community’s willingness to intervene in the Congo with its reluctance to confront French colonialism in Algeria. For Castro, however, the question of liberation extended beyond the formal end of colonial rule. He declared: “We are, therefore, on the side of the Algerian people, as we are on the remaining colonial peoples in Africa, and on the side of those who are discriminated against in the Union of South Africa. Similarly, we are on the side of those peoples that wish to be free, not only politically, for it is very easy to acquire a flag, a coat of arms, an anthem, and a color on the map, but also economically free, for there is one truth which we should all recognize as being of primary importance, namely, that there can be no political independence unless there is economic independence, that political independence without economic independence is a lie; we therefore support the aspirations of all countries to be free politically and economically. Freedom does not consist in the possession of a flag, a coat of arms, and representation in the United Nations.” The Congo and Algeria became the central proposition that would underpin Cuba’s later engagement with Africa. Five years later, in 1965, Che Guevara led a Cuban contingent into the Congo to support the revolutionary struggle directly. The mission did not achieve the victory Havana had hoped for, but its historical significance lay on the fact that Cuba had begun making a direct material commitment to the African struggles. Internationalism at full scale Nothing captures the scale of that commitment like Angola. When Portuguese colonial rule collapsed in 1974, Angola fractured into a three-way civil war, drawn deeper into crisis when South Africa’s apartheid government invaded Namibia to crush the Soviet and Cuban-backed MPLA before it could consolidate power. Castro’s answer was Operation Carlota, named for an enslaved woman who led a Cuban uprising in 1843, a deliberate act of historical framing that tied the mission to Cuba’s own history of Black resistance. Cuban troops helped halt the South African advance on Luanda and secured the MPLA’s survival at independence. Over the sixteen years that followed, hundreds of thousands of Cuban personnel rotated through Angola, fighting, dying, and building an air and armored presence far beyond what a country of Cuba’s size should have been able to sustain against a superpower’s embargo. The decisive moment came at Cuito Cuanavale in 1987–88. The battle broke the myth of apartheid South Africa’s military invincibility, shifted the regional balance of power, and helped force the negotiations that led to Namibian independence and South Africa’s withdrawal from Angola. It is difficult to overstate what that meant for the anti-apartheid movement, a small, blockaded Caribbean nation that had offered enormous solidarity and sacrifice. African leaders praise Fidel Fidel’s charisma, political conviction and commitment to revolutionary internationalism brought him into close contact with some of Africa’s leaders and revolutionaries, including Kwame Nkrumah, Julius Nyerere, Samora Machel, Agostinho Neto, Amílcar Cabral, Ahmed Sékou Touré, and Thomas Sankara. These relationships were based on a wider political convergence around anti-colonialism, national liberation, socialism, Pan-Africanism and resistance to imperialism. While Western narratives have often presented a contested picture of Fidel Castro and his legacy, there is far less ambiguity in the memory of many African liberation movements and peoples about what Fidel and Cuba represented. For those who experienced colonialism, apartheid and foreign intervention, Cuba’s support was not an abstract Cold War alignment. It was material solidarity. Perhaps with the passage of time, the historical record will allow an even fuller appreciation of what Fidel and the Cuban people did for Africa. Read more: Cuban solidarity with Africa was ‘never rhetorical, it was practical ’ When Nelson Mandela met Fidel after his release from prison, his admiration was unmistakable, and it was rooted in something more profound than gratitude for military assistance. Mandela repeatedly pointed to the breadth of Cuba’s contribution to African liberation, the soldiers who fought alongside African forces, but also the doctors, teachers, engineers, and technicians who worked across the continent. Cuban internationalism was never reducible to arms shipments. It was an offer of human capacity, knowledge, skills and institutions to societies attempting to overcome colonialism and transform themselves. And in many respects, this civilian commitment outlasted the military one. Cuban troops eventually withdrew from Angola, but medical and educational cooperation continued into the 1990s, even as Cuba itself entered the severe economic crisis of the Special Period following the collapse of the Soviet Union. Cuba continued to send doctors and other professionals abroad at a time when its own people were facing severe shortages at home. By 1998, addressing the South African Parliament, Fidel put a number to the military dimension of this commitment; 381,432 Cuban soldiers and officers had served alongside African forces in struggles for independence or against foreign aggression. It represents the scale of a small country’s material and human commitment, a continent that Cuba was never compelled to assist, but whose struggles Fidel and the Cuban Revolution regarded as inseparable from their own. Castro’s African legacy was built on a simple, unfashionable conviction, that no nation is free in isolation, and that solidarity, to mean anything, has to cost something. A century after his birth and ten years after his death, that is still the reason his name is spoken with respect from the continent. If Africa remembers what Cuba did for its liberation struggles, then perhaps the time has also come for Africa to ask what it can do for Cuba. Cuba is today facing an economic crisis and the continuing weight of the US blockade and sanctions. Yet the country that once sent soldiers, doctors, teachers and technicians to Africa when it had very little of its own still carries the consequences of that commitment. If internationalism means anything, then solidarity must also be reciprocal. Africa’s remembrance of Fidel should therefore also be a call for concrete solidarity with the Cuban people today, for defending Cuba’s sovereignty, opposing the blockade and refusing to allow a country that contributed so much to African liberation to face its present difficulties in isolation. articles.title: US empire in decline? Vijay Prashad on Iran war backfire
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Is rampant militarism accelerating US decline rather than reversing it? Vijay Prashad, executive director of the Tricontinental Institute for Social Research, argues Trump’s war on Iran has exposed the hard limits of American military and diplomatic power, as Washington faces strategic defeat by Tehran it refuses to admit. Prashad breaks down why Gulf states, most recently Oman, are coming to understand why hosting US bases is more liability than protection, given the new Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey — a security pact built entirely apart from US interests, with Egypt reportedly circling to join. He explains why Iraq’s next moves could determine whether the region stabilizes or escalates further. After US strikes on Syria, Iraq, Yemen, Lebanon, and Palestine via Israel, why would any country still trust the United States? And Prashad points to East Asia, where the Pacific is left without a single carrier given the USS Abraham Lincoln’s record 260-day deployment to the Gulf, and where Tokyo and Seoul may be taking notes on the lesson Gulf states just learned.
